```{r data-loading}
# ============================================================================
# Trial-level data loading.
# Walks raw_data/<Site>/<subject_id>/<block>/<block>_<subject>.csv
# and stacks every trial from every subject into one long data frame.
#
# Location of the data with the UChicago & Oberlin data:
RAW_DATA_PATH <- "raw_data"
# ============================================================================

# Loads one block of trials 
# Each subject has 2 blocks (every subject did both blocks, but not necesarily in this order)
#   1 - Full Sentence
#   2- Imagined Sentence
# Block CSV columns:
#   Subject Number, Block Scheme, Stimulus Number, Stimulus Type, Subject Response,
#   Play Count, Trial Start Timestamp, Play Button Clicked Timestamp,
#   Audio Start Timestamp, Audio End Timestamp, Subject Response Timestamp
# R's implementation of read.csv() turns the spaces in column names into dots/periods so 
#   we can reference a column named "Stimulus Type" via "df$Stimulus.Type"
load_subject_block <- function(site, subject_id, block_type) {

  # Each subject has two trial-level CSVs, one per block, with 149 rows each
  path <- file.path(RAW_DATA_PATH, site, subject_id, block_type,
                    paste0(block_type, "_", subject_id, ".csv"))

  # Read the csv into a df
  df <- read.csv(path)

  # Build a df with just the columns we care about
  # subject is site-prefixed to ensure global-uniqueness across experimental sites
  #   correct      = 1 iff subject's response matched the experimenter's label
  #   said_target  = 1 iff subject pressed "target" on this trial
  #   true_target  = 1 iff the experimenter labeled this trial a target
  data.frame(
    
    # uchicago or oberlin
    site = site, 
    
    # Subject number (here we prepend the experimental site for uniqueness)
    subject = paste(site, subject_id, sep = "_"),
    
    # Which trial the subject was on (trial 1, trial 50, trial n, ...)
    trial_num = seq_len(nrow(df)),
    
    # Which specific stimulus the subject heard on this trial
    # I need this to join the per-stimulus Pearson r values onto trials later
    stimulus_number = df$Stimulus.Number,
    
    # Which of the two block we are on (full sentence vs imagined sentence)
    block_scheme = df$Block.Scheme,
    
    # regardless of whether it is a target or a distarctor, did the subject identify it correctly
    correct = as.integer(df$Stimulus.Type == df$Subject.Response),
    
    # 1 if the subejct claimed it was a target, 0 if they claimed distractor 
    said_target = as.integer(df$Subject.Response == "target"),
    
    # 1 if it was actually a target, 0 if it was actually a distractor
    # ("actually" means that we, the experimenters, had labelled it as a target vs a distractor)
    true_target = as.integer(df$Stimulus.Type  == "target")
  )
}

# Loads the order in which the subject saw the blocks (full sentence and imagined sentence)
# Summary CSV columns:
#   Subject Number, Block 1, Block 1 D-Prime, Block 2, Block 2 D-Prime
# After read.csv these become Block.1, Block.1.D.Prime, etc...
load_block_order <- function(site, subject_id) {

  # The summary_data file tells us which block ran first
  path <- file.path(RAW_DATA_PATH, site, subject_id, paste0("summary_data_", subject_id, ".csv"))

  # Read the summary data csv which contains the block order
  summary_data <- read.csv(path)

  # Construct a summary data dataframe with....
  #   1) the subject number, site-prefixed so it's globally unique
  #         (raw format is MMDDYYYYXXX where XXX is left filled with 0s
  #         representing which subject of the day; e.g. 002 means the 2nd
  #         subject of that day; same MMDDYYYYXXX could in principle appear
  #         at both sites so we prepend the site)
  #   2) the experimental site (UChicago vs Oberlin)
  #   3) the block order (which block was 1st, which was 2nd)
  data.frame(
    subject                 = paste(site, subject_id, sep = "_"),
    site                    = site,
    full_sentence_order     = ifelse(summary_data$Block.1 == "full_sentence",     1L, 2L),
    imagined_sentence_order = ifelse(summary_data$Block.1 == "imagined_sentence", 1L, 2L)
    
    # Note: "1L" means "set this to the number '1' but make sure it is an integer
    #   because if we just wrote "1" then R would store it as a double, which could lead
    #   to annoying floating point issues if we indeed just want an integer (also not memory efficient)
  )
}


# Walk both sites, both blocks, and all subjects
all_trials <- list()
all_orders <- list()

# Iterate over the experimental sites
for (site in c("Oberlin", "UChicago")) {

  # List all of the subject data folders
  subj_dirs <- list.dirs(file.path(RAW_DATA_PATH, site), recursive = FALSE, full.names = FALSE)

  # Iterate over each subject data folder
  for (subject_id in subj_dirs) {

    # Iterate over both blocks
    for (block in c("full_sentence", "imagined_sentence")) {

      # Add the subject's trials as a LIST to the list of all trials
      all_trials[[length(all_trials) + 1]] <- load_subject_block(site, subject_id, block)
    }

    # Add the subject's block order/summary data as a LIST to the existing list of block orders
    all_orders[[length(all_orders) + 1]] <- load_block_order(site, subject_id)
  }
}

# Since each entry is a list, we flatten the lists to just be a single list of trials/block orders
# The previous loop produced, for example, all_trials [[subject 1's trials], [subject 2's trials], ...]
#   and this turns it from a list of lists into one flat list [subject, 1's, trials, subject, 2's, trials, ...]
trials <- do.call(rbind, all_trials)
orders <- do.call(rbind, all_orders)

# Attach block_order_index to each trial (getting a little SQL with it)
# Basically, just join the two lists based on subject number, which is present in every item in both lists
# So every trial gets two new columns (full_sentence_order & imagined_sentence_order)
# This is what the data looks like after this block:
# subject              block_scheme         ...  full_sentence_order  imagined_sentence_order
# Oberlin_03032025001  full_sentence        ...  2                    1
# Oberlin_03032025001  full_sentence        ...  2                    1
# Oberlin_03032025001  imagined_sentence    ...  2                    1
#
trials <- trials |>
  left_join(orders, by = c("subject", "site")) |>
  mutate(block_order_index = ifelse(block_scheme == "full_sentence", full_sentence_order, imagined_sentence_order)) |>
  select(-full_sentence_order, -imagined_sentence_order)

# Dummy / sum coding for predictors:
#   block_dummy: 0 = imagined, 1 = full        (so bBlock = Full effect)
#   site_dummy:  0 = UChicago, 1 = Oberlin     (so bSite  = Oberlin effect)
#   order_dummy: 0 = first,    1 = second      (so bOrder = practice effect)
#   true_target_centered: -0.5 = distractor, +0.5 = target
#   We center this so that the slope on it IS d' in classical units when probit link 
#     is used; the intercept becomes the criterion at the average trial.)
trials <- trials |>
  mutate(
    block_dummy          = as.integer(block_scheme == "full_sentence"),
    site_dummy           = as.integer(site == "Oberlin"),
    order_dummy          = as.integer(block_order_index == 2),
    true_target_centered = ifelse(true_target == 1, 0.5, -0.5)
  )

# Build a subject-level integer index for ulam (1..N_subjects)
# subject is now globally unique (site-prefixed), so joining on subject alone is safe
# Ehh it is experimental data so I am certain it is not safe. But whatever, c'est la vie
subj_lookup <- trials |>
  distinct(subject, site) |>
  arrange(site, subject) |>
  mutate(subject_idx = row_number())

trials <- trials |> left_join(subj_lookup |> select(subject, subject_idx), by = "subject")

cat(sprintf("Loaded %d trials across %d subjects (%d Oberlin, %d UChicago)\n",
            nrow(trials),
            n_distinct(trials$subject),
            n_distinct(trials$subject[trials$site == "Oberlin"]),
            n_distinct(trials$subject[trials$site == "UChicago"])))
head(trials)
tail(trials)
```

```{r pearson-r-loading}
# ============================================================================
# Per-stimulus Pearson r values (precomputed in the stimulus pipeline so not
# much new computation here) and then join these values onto trials.
# ============================================================================
# Each noise clip was scored against the wall.wav template back when the
# stimulus set was assembled, and the scalar r values live in two CSVs:
#   high_correlation_stimuli.csv  -- 153 targets, r in [0.072, 0.090]  (3 are example targs)
#   low_correlation_stimuli.csv   -- 153 distractors, |r| < 1.5e-6  (3 are example dists)
# Joining these onto our trials by Stimulus.Number gives the continuous
# per-trial r-to-target value (so far we have only the experimenter label binary
# target/distractor label). This continuous similarity is what M4/M5 will
# use to examine label-flipped subjects (negative slope on r) separately
# from noise subjects (~zero slope on r) without the manual dprime flip that
# I have tried before but often been bothered by.
target_corr <- read.csv(file.path(RAW_DATA_PATH, "audio_stimuli", "correlation_csvs", "high_correlation_stimuli.csv"))
distr_corr  <- read.csv(file.path(RAW_DATA_PATH, "audio_stimuli", "correlation_csvs", "low_correlation_stimuli.csv"))

# Stack the two correlation tables into one lookup
stim_r <- rbind(target_corr, distr_corr)

# Join r_score onto every trial by stimulus_number
trials <- trials |> left_join(stim_r, by = c("stimulus_number" = "stimulus_number"))

# Make sure the join worked (targets avg should be ~0.08, distractors ~ 0, and no NAs)
# To Future OCD David: PRESENT DAVID CAN CONFIRM THIS ACTUALLY RETURNS EXPECTED VALUES
# DONT wASTE TIME WONDERING
trials |>
  group_by(true_target) |>
  summarize(
    mean_r = mean(r_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_r   = sd(r_score,   na.rm = TRUE),
    min_r  = min(r_score,  na.rm = TRUE),
    max_r  = max(r_score,  na.rm = TRUE),
    n_na   = sum(is.na(r_score))
  )

# Center the pearson r score across all trials so the slope on it has the
# interpretation "log-odds shift per unit deviation from average trial's r"
# Targets end up around +0.04 and distractors around -0.04 after centering
trials <- trials |> mutate(sim_to_target = r_score - mean(r_score, na.rm = TRUE))
```

```{r raw-dprime-and-flip}
# ============================================================================
# Pre-compute d' per (subject, block) and per subject (pooled
# across blocks).
# ============================================================================

# z() with log-linear correction so subjects with Hit Rate = 1 or 
# False Alarm Rate = 0 don't blow up since d' is a difference of their Z-Scores
safe_z <- function(p, n) {
  qnorm((p * n + 0.5) / (n + 1))
}

# ===================================================================================
# ===================================================================================
# Per (subject, block) d'
# I've been working through some functional programming languages lately (OCaml & Haskell)
# Been experimenting with this sort of notation (the pipe operator is also in OCaml, but slightly different)... 
# so what is it? More or less we are just using postfix notation and doing a different method of applying arguments to functions.
# Whereas in OCaml x |> f y curries to f(y, x), in R x |> f y curries to f(x, y). Not a big issue but don't get it switched!!
# The imperative version of this is ....
#   subj_block_dprime <- mutate(summarize(group_by(trials, site, subject, subject_idx, block_scheme), ...), ...)
# The general approach is common to SQL type queries/transformations and follows a typical ETL (extract, transform, load to central location)
# pipeline. In R terminology this translates to split (into groups), apply (transformations), combine (into a cleaned data object)
# This is perfectly well reflected in the order of functions mentioned above. 
#   1. We "group_by()" experimental site, subject number, subject index, block type (This is the "split")
#   2. We "summarize()" to reduce each block to a single row so 2 rows per subject (This is the "apply")
#   3. We "mutate()" to add a derived d' column. Ill admit this actually doesn't fit in to this schema but I wrote this entire pompous block already so im not rewriting it.
subj_block_dprime <- trials |>
  group_by(site, subject, subject_idx, block_scheme) |>
  summarize(
    n_target     = sum(true_target == 1),
    n_distractor = sum(true_target == 0),
    hit_rate     = mean(said_target[true_target == 1]),
    fa_rate      = mean(said_target[true_target == 0]),
    .groups      = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(dprime = safe_z(hit_rate, n_target) - safe_z(fa_rate, n_distractor)) |>
  mutate(flip_block = as.integer(dprime < 0))

# Print the table
subj_block_dprime

# ===================================================================================
# ===================================================================================

# ===================================================================================
# ===================================================================================
# Pooled d' per subject (across both blocks). This is the number that
# decides whether the subject is "recognizing the difference between categories but got the labels flipped" for the M4 analysis.
subj_dprime <- trials |>
  group_by(site, subject, subject_idx) |>
  summarize(
    n_target     = sum(true_target == 1),
    n_distractor = sum(true_target == 0),
    hit_rate     = mean(said_target[true_target == 1]),
    fa_rate      = mean(said_target[true_target == 0]),
    .groups      = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    dprime_pooled = safe_z(hit_rate, n_target) - safe_z(fa_rate, n_distractor),
    flip_subject  = as.integer(dprime_pooled < 0)
  )
# ===================================================================================
# ===================================================================================
# Graphing for how many subjects we want to flip dprimes for
# 1. Whole experiment
overall_tab <- subj_dprime |>
  count(flip_subject) |>
  mutate(Block = "Overall")
# 2. Full sentence block
full_tab <- subj_block_dprime |>
  filter(block_scheme == "full_sentence") |>
  count(flip_block) |>
  mutate(Block = "Full Sentence") |>
  rename(flip_subject = flip_block)

# 3. Imagined sentence block
imagined_tab <- subj_block_dprime |>
  filter(block_scheme == "imagined_sentence") |>
  count(flip_block) |>
  mutate(Block = "Imagined Sentence") |>
  rename(flip_subject = flip_block)

# Print the table of flips by overall dprim, and by block type
overall_tab
full_tab
imagined_tab

# Arranges from high to low on pooled dprime
subj_dprime |> arrange(dprime_pooled)
subj_dprime
```

```{r ulam-data-prep}
# ============================================================================
# Build the slim list of data for easy use in  ulam.
# ============================================================================

# Here we are reorganizing trials. We do the following....
# left join the subject dprime on subject number and also blockscheme depending on circumstance
#     (since we want to check this for each block and for the overall dprimes)
trials <- trials |>
  
  #  left join on "subject" for experiment wide analysis
  left_join(subj_dprime       |> select(subject, flip_subject), by = "subject") |>
  
  #  left join on "subject" and "block_scheme" for block-by-block analysis  
  left_join(subj_block_dprime |> select(subject, block_scheme, flip_block), by = c("subject", "block_scheme")) |>
  
  # Generate new columns (one for experiment level flip, one for block level flip) evaluating to
  #   the opposite values for subject response (target = 1, distractor = 0) if subject's dprime < 0 
  #   Otherwise (subject dprime >= 0) we keep things exactly the same
  mutate(
    said_target_flipped       = ifelse(flip_subject == 1, 1L - said_target, said_target),
    said_target_flipped_block = ifelse(flip_block   == 1, 1L - said_target, said_target)
  )


# Build the final "slim" list with the data for easy data operation
slim <- list(
  
  # Num stimuli correctly identified (independent of whether target or distractor)
  correct = as.integer(trials$correct),
  
  # Number of times the subject said that a stimulus was a target (indpendent of if they are correct)
  said_target = as.integer(trials$said_target),
  
  # Number of times subject said a stimulus was a target and the stimulus was a target (accd to the experimenter)
  true_target = as.numeric(trials$true_target_centered),
  
  # Centered per-trial Pearson r with wall.wav.
  # Slope on this is beta_truetarget --- the alignment metric M4/M5 use to
  # detect label-flipped subjects (negative slope = anti-aligned with target).
  sim_to_target = as.numeric(trials$sim_to_target),
  
  # Name of the block (full sentence vs imagined sentence)
  block = as.integer(trials$block_dummy),
  
  # experimental site (uchicago vs oberlin)
  site = as.integer(trials$site_dummy),
  
  # Order in which the subject received this block 
  order = as.integer(trials$order_dummy),
  
  # Less relevant, but whatever 1, ..., N_subjects index this subject received
  #   I am ocd so i enjoy convergent checks on my data to ensure no funny business
  subject_idx = as.integer(trials$subject_idx),
  
  # Total number of subjects
  # Nice to have this in every trial row if we ever need easy access to this number
  # Not the most efficient, but hey, let's live a little
  N_sub = as.integer(max(trials$subject_idx))
)

```


```{r m4-data-prep}
# ============================================================================
# Data prep for the full-sentence-only subset for M4 and M5
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Drop all imagined_sentence trials. No flipping. Per-trial sim_to_target
# (centered Pearson r against wall.wav) carries the sign-preserving signal
# instead of any manual flip operation.
# 
# we have the existing result about oberlin full sentence and at both experimental
# sites we have either full sentence significance or trending in that direction
#  (results consistent with the same effect but underpowered at uchicago)
# so there is a reason to think that the addition of imagined sentence will be
# polluting the analysis with noise.
# The quesiton I am interested in here is whether the data is consistent with
# "some subjects were able to recognize there were two groups of stimuli 
# and discern between those two groups stimuli but they just got the labels flipped...
# This would result in a negative dprime spike in a dprime/subject count histogram
# which LOOKS LIKE A NORMAL DISTRIBUTION but is also consistent with the hypothesis 
# I am testing here. 
# In order to address this, we need to look at data where subjects were able to actually
# do the task, because the hypothesis is not testable when no subjects successfully do the task.
# In that case it is all noise and you can't ask about subjects who were doing the task (partially) correctly
#   but made the mistake of flipping the labels". As a result, it is justified that we remove the 
#   imagined sentence block's data since it does not seem that anybody could reliably do this block.
trials_full <- trials |> filter(block_scheme == "full_sentence")


# Build the slim list for the full-sentence-only models (M4 and M5).
# Block dummy is omitted since block is constant in this subset.
slim_full <- list(
  
  # raw said_target
  said_target = as.integer(trials_full$said_target),
  
  # centered target label (+/- 0.5) slope on this is d'
  true_target = as.numeric(trials_full$true_target_centered),
  
  # centered per-trial Pearson r with wall.wav.
  # slope on this is beta_truetarget; sign tells flipped vs correct vs noise.
  sim_to_target = as.numeric(trials_full$sim_to_target),
  
  # site dummy (Oberlin = 1, UChicago = 0)
  site = as.integer(trials_full$site_dummy),
  
  # order dummy (2nd block = 1, 1st block = 0)
  order = as.integer(trials_full$order_dummy),
  
  # subject index (still 1 thru N_subjects since every subject did the full_sentence block)
  subject_idx = as.integer(trials_full$subject_idx),
  
  # total subjects
  N_sub = as.integer(max(trials_full$subject_idx))
)

# sanity check the trial count
cat(sprintf("Full-sentence-only subset: %d trials across %d subjects\n", length(slim_full$said_target), slim_full$N_sub))
```

# 1. Introduction

**Write 2-3 paragraphs of introduction/background on your research question.**

- Why is your research question interesting/important and how does it fit into the existing literature?

- Please include parenthetical citations in the introduction and APA-style references at the end.

____________________________

Auditory hallucinations (AH) are defined as the perception of sound without a corresponding physical stimulus. Typically regarded as a symptom of psychosis,  auditory hallucinations also occur in psychiatrically healthy adults. The experiences of healthy and clinical voice-hearers differ enough that researchers have argued for a continuum running from everyday hallucination-proneness into clinical psychosis (Johns & Van Os, 2001; Hill & Linden, 2013). What distinguishes people who experience AH from those who don't? One candidate mechanism is top-down sensitivity in perception. Bayesian-brain accounts hold that the percept on any given trial is a posterior combining bottom-up sensory evidence with a top-down prior shaped by expectation, attention, and imagery (Friston, 2010; Powers, Mathys, & Corlett, 2017); when bottom-up evidence is weak (as in this experiment), the posterior is dominated by the prior, and listeners whose priors are more sharply tuned or whose attention more readily latches onto signal-like structure may be more likely to "hear" something in noise (Bentall & Slade, 1985; Aleman & Larøi, 2008). Several converging lines of evidence point this direction. Merckelbach and Van De Ven (2001) told 47 undergraduates that the song "White Christmas" might be embedded in white noise played through their headphones; the song wasn't there, but 32% reported hearing it, and the reporters scored higher on the Launay-Slade Hallucination Scale and on fantasy proneness. Luhrmann, Nusbaum, and Thisted (2010) found that voice-hearing in an Evangelical Christian sample was predicted by Tellegen Absorption Scale scores rather than by religiosity per se, suggesting that the propensity to be absorbed in mental imagery (this is NOT the motivation to hear voices) was what differentiated voice-hearers from non-voice-hearers. And Gosselin and Schyns (2003) showed that observers' classification images for letters they "saw" in pure visual noise aggregated to actual letter shapes, evidence that what they "saw" was being guided by an internal target template rather than by stimulus features. Across these results the pattern is consistent: top-down expectation can systematically shape what listeners perceive in noise, and individual differences in that susceptibility track hallucination-relevant traits.

The dataset I'm analyzing was collected by researchers at the APEX Lab at UChicago and by Connor Daley at Oberlin, originally for Arwen Bare's senior honors thesis on this top-down hypothesis (IRB #24-1770). The paradigm is a forced-choice signal-detection task in noise. 26 undergraduates (16 Oberlin, 10 UChicago) listened to short white-noise clips on each trial and decided whether each clip "contained" the target word *wall*, extracted from a clean recording of the carrier sentence "The picture hung on the wall." The clips aren't truly featureless: roughly 2.8 million candidate white-noise clips were generated from quantum-random (ANU QRNG API) seeds and scored by Pearson correlation against the target waveform, with the experimentally-labeled targets drawn from the high-correlation tail (top 153 clips, $r \in [0.072, 0.090]$) and the distractors from the near-zero-correlation tail ($|r| < 1.5 \times 10^{-6}$). So the targets and distractors do differ, reliably above chance, but just barely. The highest rated target (according to pearson r) results in less than a 1/3rd of a percent of variance explained. 

The full_sentence (perception) block supports the subject's prior with explicit perceptual input: subjects hear "The picture hung on the" in the original speaker's voice before each noise clip. The imagined_sentence (imagery) block strips that support, requiring subjects to imagine the carrier phrase themselves before clicking to play the noise. If top-down expectation is what drives detection in this paradigm, the perceptual scaffold should produce more reliable detection than imagery alone. A repeated-measures ANOVA on $d'$ found a significant main effect of Group (Oberlin > UChicago, $p = 0.03$) but no main effect of Block Type and no interaction, with a per-cell follow-up showing Oberlin above chance in the perception block ($p = 0.001$) and UChicago at chance. These results hold up to non-parametric statistical tests such as Wilcoxon vs chance, Mann–Whitney across sites, paired Wilcoxon for the within-subject Full–Imagined contrast. All statistical tests returned the same results: Oberlin full_sentence is robustly above chance ($d' = 0.137$, $p = 0.001$, Cohen's $d \approx 1.0$), every other cell is at or near chance, and the within-subject Full–Imagined comparison to Imagined-Sentence is in the predicted direction in every reporting group (UChicago, Oberlin, Unified) but reaches $p < 0.05$ in none.

There are three things that subject-mean-level NHT analysis can't do that a Bayesian multilevel approach can. First, each subject contributes ~298 trials (off by one error in my code, twice!), and collapsing those to a single number throws away the within-subject trial variance that the multilevel framework can use to tighten estimates. Second, "trending only" comparisons ($p \in [0.05, 0.20]$, $d$ medium-to-large) deserve a continuous evidence read rather than a binary reject/fail-to-reject. Layered on top of $d'$, a two-component mixture (engaged trials vs. lapse-guessing trials, in the style of HW4's `m_ZI` model) lets me ask whether some apparent noise in the data is actually inattention rather than insensitivity. And the "are some subjects capable but label-flipped?" question is of importance. The cleanest way to ask it without the selection-on-outcome bias of pre-flipping responses is to give each subject a slope on the continuous per-trial r-to-target value alongside their d' on the binary label: a flipped subject has a negative slope, a noise subject's slope is ~0, and a correctly-responding subject's slope is positive. I run this on the full_sentence subset (where our previous analyses showed that genuine signal exists. We exclude the imagined block because it essentially noise for every subject) as M4. M5 then puts an explicit 3-component mixture prior on the subject-level (d, beta) pair. The 3 components are noise centered at (0,0), correct at (+mu, +mu), flipped at (-mu, -mu), reflecting the three hypothesized types of subjects (cant do task, can do task, can do task but got the labels flipped). and asks whether the data actually "wants" that discrete class structure or whether continuous noise around a simpler model is enough.

## 2A. Making your DAG(s)

**Draw the DAG(s) of your research question using the daggity tool McElreath provides in rethinking (i.e., do not just write Y<-X<-Z->A<-B; instead, lay out your DAG in space with daggity). Any variables that are included in your statistical model should be included in your DAG (though multi-level model params may not). Your DAG may not be very complicated if your study is experimental.**

```{r dag-build}
# ============================================================================
# DAG for the auditory superstitious perception task
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three things are randomized in this paradigm:
#     1 - Block (full sentence vs imagined sentence),
#     2 - Block Order (the order in which the blocks are presented)
#     3 - Stimulus Type (whether the stimulus is a target or distractor).
# Experimental Site (UChicago vs Oberlin) is observational since the subejcts 
#   were not randomly assigned to Oberlin vs UChicago

# In this DAG U is a latent unobserved subject-level variable. 

# U includes a bunch of, perhaps estimable via questionnaires, but we arent doing
# questionnnaires in hthis analysis: 

# This include but is not limited to:
#     1 - Musical training (Oberlin has a famous conservatory)
#     2 - Auditory imagery ability/propensity (BAIS C/V questionnaires)
#     3 - dissociative tendencies (DES-II scale/questionnaire) 
#     4 - hallucination-proneness traits (LSHS, TAS), attention on the day
#     5 - Hearing acuity (related to 1)
# 
# (Experimental) Site --> U represents the possibility that the these two
#   populations differ on these aspects
# ============================================================================
sp_dag <- dagitty("dag{
    Block       -> Sensitivity
    BlockOrder  -> Sensitivity
    TrueTarget  -> SaidTarget
    Sensitivity -> SaidTarget
    Criterion   -> SaidTarget
    Site        -> Sensitivity
    U           -> Sensitivity
    U           -> Criterion
    Site        -> U
}")

# Follow a Left-Right axis format:
#   - experimental knobs on the left
#   - latent stuff on the right, 
#   - observed trial outcome (SaidTarget) bottom-right
#
# At the end of the day, 3 variables hypothetically contribute to whether 
# the subject claims that a given stimulus is a target or not...
#   1) Was it labelled a target? (More signal present accd to Pearson R)
#   2) Criterion/Resppnse Bias (Subejct predisposed to one response vs the other)
#   3) Sensitivity (Can the subject hear a difference, pick up on signal, etc...)
# 
# Note: Flipping the labels for targets vs distractors is still a sign of sensitivity.
#     since they can still tell the difference between the two categories. All stimuli
#     sound like white noise and the idea/interesting thing is that anyone can pick up 
#     on such little signal. You can decompose a successful subject (high d') into someone who... 
# 
#         1) knows the difference between the group of stimuli that we labelled
#             "targets" and the group of stimuli that we labelled "distractors"
# 
#                                     AND
# 
#         2) Know which of these groups was meant to be "targets" and which of these
#             groups was meant to be distractors.
# 
# 
#   It is certainly possible that a subejct can do #1 ("hey there are two groups!")
#   but not do #2 ("I know there is a difference, but they both sound like static, 
#     so I am just going to guess about which one I should call 'target' and which one
#     I should call 'distractor'")  
#                                  ? ?
#                                   ?
#                                \__O__/
#     The subject ----->            |         <----- The subject  
#                                   |
#                                  / \
#                     
# 
#  OHHH my GOOOOD why wont these suckers just line up the way i want them
coordinates(sp_dag) <- list(
  x = c(Block = 0, BlockOrder = 0, Site = 2.5, U = 2.5,
        Sensitivity = 1.5, Criterion = 1.5,
        TrueTarget = 0, SaidTarget = 3),
  y = c(Block = 0, BlockOrder = 1, Site = 0, U = 1,
        Sensitivity = 0.4, Criterion = 1.3,
```

## 2B. Interpreting your DAG(s)

Please answer the following three questions:

- Is your study experimental or observational?

- Based on your DAG(s), do you think you will be able to make causal claims?

- Are there any unobserved variables that you need to also consider?

____________________________

The study is has both experimental and behavorial components. Three things are randomly assigned and thus meet the criteria for "experimental": 
  1 - Block: full vs imagined, within-subject, counterbalanced order
  2 - BlockOrder: which block the subject sees first, between-subject randomized
  3 - Stimulus Type ("TrueTarget"): The experimenter's per-trial label which is randomized within block. 
  
In principle we can make some causal claims because randomization breaks any incoming arrow from upstream variables, including the unobserved subject latent U. By contrast, Site (Oberlin vs UChicago) is observational since subjects self-selected through the recruitment process so its effect on Sensitivity is confounded by whatever U-style differences exist between the two undergraduate populations.

I expect to be able to make causal claims about how the manipulation affects sensitivity (as measured by d'): does Block actually raise d'? does block-order affect d'? 

For Site I'll be more cautious since I can only describe the *association* between site and sensitivity after partialling out BlockOrder, but I can't rule out U as a confounder. The most important unobserved variable is U: a latent subject-level traits that drive both Sensitivity (how well subjects can pick up on the very weak Pearson-r structure separating targets from distractors) and Criterion (their bias toward saying "target"). Our experimental design tried to identify and quantify several plausible components of U: musical training (Oberlin is partly a conservatory, and many of her Oberlin participants self reported playing instruments), auditory imagery vividness, ability for sustained attention, dissociative tendencies, and hallucination-proneness traits as measured by TAS / LSHS / DESII / BAIS / VHQ. None of these is observed in the present analysis (I'm not conditioning on questionnaires for analyses here because we already did one round of analyses and I am using this assignment to do some further analyses), so they will live in U  for this analysis. The "lapse" parameter in M3/M4/M5 is capturing the attentional component of U specifically.

## 2C. Parameters that you are trying to estimate

**What parameters are you trying to estimate?**

____________________________

The main parameters I am estimating, grouped by what they represent:

**Population-level sensitivity:**

- **$\bar d$ (population mean d$'$)**: how sensitive the average subject is against the reference cell (UChicago / imagined / first block). $\bar d = 0$ means no discrimination on average.
- **$b_{BT}$ (Block $\times$ TrueTarget)**: how much $d'$ changes from imagined to full_sentence. Positive means full_sentence raises sensitivity.
- **$b_{ST}$ (Site $\times$ TrueTarget)**: how much $d'$ shifts from UChicago to Oberlin. Observational, so I will be cautious about causal interpretation.
- **$b_{OT}$ (Order $\times$ TrueTarget)**: practice effect on sensitivity (2nd block vs 1st block).
- **$b_{BST}$ (Block $\times$ Site $\times$ TrueTarget)**: the three-way that is the Oberlin-and-full_sentence $d'$ bump on top of the additive Site and Block effects. This is the closest single coefficient to the "Oberlin full_sentence above chance" effect from the NHT that i want to revist in a bayesian contetxt.
- **$b_{BOT}$ (Block $\times$ Order $\times$ TrueTarget)**: does the imagined sentence to full sentence performance improvement trend depend on whether full_sentence came first or second?

**M1-specific log-odds parameters (M1 is estimating log odds of correct, not the $d'$/criterion, so these don't map exactly to the parameters above):**

- **$a\_bar$ (grand-mean log-odds of being correct)**: average log-odds of a correct response in the reference cell (UChicago / imagined / first block). $a\_bar = 0$ means 50% accuracy on average; positive values mean above chance.
- **$bB\_bar$ (population Block slope)**: log-odds shift from imagined to full_sentence. M1's analogue of $b_{BT}$ in M2--M5, but it mixes sensitivity and criterion because M1's DV is `correct` rather than `said_target`.
- **$bSite$, $bOrder$ (Site, Order main effects)**: log-odds shifts for Oberlin vs UChicago and 2nd-block vs 1st-block.
- **$bB\_site$, $bB\_order$ (Block $\times$ Site and Block $\times$ Order interactions)**: whether the Block effect on log-odds-correct depends on site or order. $bB\_site$ is the closest single coefficient in M1 to the "Oberlin full_sentence above chance" effect.
- **$\sigma_a$, $\sigma_{bB}$ (between-subject SDs on intercept and Block slope)**: how much subjects vary in baseline accuracy and in the size of the Block effect.

**M4-specific population-level alignment (sign-preserving flip metric):**

- **$\bar\beta$ (population mean alignment with the true target)**: the average strength with which subjects' responses track the trial-by-trial Pearson $r$ between the noise clip and the wall template (`sim_to_target`). Sign-preserving: positive $\bar\beta$ means subjects on average say "target" more often on trials whose noise clip happens to look more like the actual `wall` waveform. Negative would mean they're anti-aligned with the target on average.
- **$\sigma_\beta$ (between-subject SD on alignment)**: how much subjects differ in their alignment with the true target. Large $\sigma_\beta$ relative to $\bar\beta$ is hopefully a better test of the flip hypothesis. We have had crude measures of this before, and I am using this assignment to try to build out some other ways of testing this. Point is I think this will be a better at discerning that subjects can be substantially positive (correct), near zero (noise), or substantially negative (flipped) even if the population mean is small.

**Population-level criterion / response bias:**

- **$\bar c$ (population criterion)**: response bias of the average subject (positive = tendency to say "target", negative = tendency to say "distractor"). Block, Site, Order can shift criterion separately from $d'$.
- **$b_B, b_S, b_O$ (Block, Site, Order main effects on criterion)**: how much criterion shifts across conditions, independent of sensitivity.
- **$b_{BS}, b_{BO}$ (Block $\times$ Site and Block $\times$ Order criterion interactions)**: whether the criterion shifts above interact.

**Between-subject variability:**

- **$\sigma_c, \sigma_d$ (between-subject SDs on criterion and sensitivity)**: how much subjects vary in their underlying $c$ and $d'$.

**Lapse:**

- **$p_{\text{lapse}}$**: the fraction of trials on which a subject is guessing 50/50 rather than using their $d'$.

**M5-specific mixture parameters (replacing the simple Normal partial pooling on $(d_s, \beta_s)$ with a three-component mirror-constrained mixture):**

- **$\mu_d, \mu_\beta$ (correct-class means)**: the location of the "correct" class in $(d, \beta)$ space. By the mirror constraint the "flipped" class lives at $(-\mu_d, -\mu_\beta)$ and the "noise" class at $(0, 0)$.
- **$\boldsymbol\pi = (\pi_{\text{noise}}, \pi_{\text{correct}}, \pi_{\text{flipped}})$ (mixing proportions)**: the population shares of each latent class. $\pi_{\text{flipped}}$ credibly above zero would be suggest evidence for the flip hypothesis.
- **$\sigma_{d,\text{sig}}, \sigma_{\beta,\text{sig}}$ (within-class SDs on the signal classes)** and **$\sigma_{d,\text{noise}}, \sigma_{\beta,\text{noise}}$ (within-class SDs on the noise class)**: how tightly each class clusters in $(d, \beta)$.
- **Per-subject latent class $z_s$ and the derived $P(z_s = k \mid \text{data})$**: which class each subject most likely belongs to (computed in the `generated quantities` block of M5's Stan code and surfaced as the `m5_class` table).

____________________________

**What statistical models will you be using and why?**

In this section, please also address the following:

- Please justify your dependent measure's distribution (i.e., your DV distribution/likelihood function) and your link function.

- Please write out your full statistical models (at least two of them) with priors for your parameters (in the format below).

- Please specify what will be different between your different models (e.g., different types of models or different priors, fixed effects vs. mixed effects, etc.).

____________________________

**Likelihood and link function.** The trial-level DV in M1 is `correct` $\in \{0,1\}$, and in M2--M5 it's `said_target` $\in \{0,1\}$. Both are Bernoulli at the trial level (no continuous DV), so the likelihood is `dbinom(1, p)`. For M1 I use the logit link (standard since effects on log-odds add linearly). For M2--M5 I use the **probit link**, which is the standard SDT parameterization. The useful property her is that with probit link and `true_target_centered` $\in \{-0.5, +0.5\}$, the slope on `true_target_centered` IS actually just $d'$. This means I can read d' directly off of the slope and compare  directly against the NHT $d'$ values.

In the equations below I use the shorthand $T_i \equiv$ `true_target_centered`$_i \in \{-0.5, +0.5\}$ and $R_i \equiv$ `sim_to_target`$_i$ (the centered per-trial Pearson r with the `wall` template). $\text{Block}_i, \text{Site}_i, \text{Order}_i$ are the $\{0, 1\}$ dummies defined in the data-loading chunk (full=1, Oberlin=1, second-block=1).

**Model 1 (`m1_acc`): multilevel logistic on accuracy.** Bayesian replication of the NHT logistic from the original thesis, but with proper partial pooling.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{correct}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i) \\
\text{logit}(p_i) &= a_{s[i]} + bB_{s[i]} \cdot \text{Block}_i + bSite \cdot \text{Site}_i + bOrder \cdot \text{Order}_i \\
&\quad + bB\_site \cdot \text{Block}_i \cdot \text{Site}_i + bB\_order \cdot \text{Block}_i \cdot \text{Order}_i \\[3pt]
a_{s} &\sim \text{Normal}(a\_bar, \sigma_a) \\
bB_{s} &\sim \text{Normal}(bB\_bar, \sigma_{bB}) \\
a\_bar &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 1.5) \\
bB\_bar &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5) \\
bSite, bOrder &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5) \\
bB\_site, bB\_order &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.3) \\
\sigma_a, \sigma_{bB} &\sim \text{Exponential}(1)
\end{aligned}
$$

**Model 2 (`m2_sdt`): multilevel SDT, no lapse.** DV switches to `said_target` and the link to probit. Per-subject criterion $c_s$ and per-subject sensitivity $d_s$. Each of Block, Site, Order gets BOTH a $d'$-shift (via interaction with $T_i$) AND a criterion shift (main effect, no $T_i$). Same for Block $\times$ Site and Block $\times$ Order. $b_{BST}$ is the three-way Block $\times$ Site $\times$ TrueTarget interaction.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{said\_target}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_i) \\
p_i &= \Phi\bigl(\,c_{s[i]} + d_{s[i]} \cdot T_i \\
&\qquad\quad + b_{BT} \cdot \text{Block}_i \cdot T_i + b_{ST} \cdot \text{Site}_i \cdot T_i + b_{OT} \cdot \text{Order}_i \cdot T_i \\
&\qquad\quad + b_{BST} \cdot \text{Block}_i \cdot \text{Site}_i \cdot T_i + b_{BOT} \cdot \text{Block}_i \cdot \text{Order}_i \cdot T_i \\
&\qquad\quad + b_{B} \cdot \text{Block}_i + b_{S} \cdot \text{Site}_i + b_{O} \cdot \text{Order}_i \\
&\qquad\quad + b_{BS} \cdot \text{Block}_i \cdot \text{Site}_i + b_{BO} \cdot \text{Block}_i \cdot \text{Order}_i\,\bigr) \\[3pt]
c_{s} &\sim \text{Normal}(\bar c, \sigma_c) \\
d_{s} &\sim \text{Normal}(\bar d, \sigma_d) \\
\bar c, \bar d &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5) \\
b_{BT}, b_{ST}, b_{OT}, b_{BST}, b_{BOT} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.3) \\
b_{B}, b_{S}, b_{O}, b_{BS}, b_{BO} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.3) \\
\sigma_c, \sigma_d &\sim \text{Exponential}(1)
\end{aligned}
$$

The Block $\times$ TrueTarget interaction $b_{BT}$ is a population-level $d'$ shift from imagined to full; the main effect $b_B$ is a criterion shift. SDT cleanly separates the two; the original NHT logistic on accuracy couldn't.

**Model 3 (`m3_sdt_mix`): M2 + lapse mixture.** Same linear predictor as M2, wrapped in a two-component mixture (engaged trials follow $\Phi(\cdot)$; lapse trials are 50/50). HW4's `m_ZI` structure.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{said\_target}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_{\text{obs},i}) \\
p_{\text{obs},i} &= (1 - p_{\text{lapse}}) \cdot \Phi(\text{linear predictor as in M2}) + p_{\text{lapse}} \cdot 0.5 \\
p_{\text{lapse}} &\sim \text{Beta}(2, 20) \\
\text{all other priors and structure as in M2}&
\end{aligned}
$$

**Model 4 (`m4_full_beta`): M3 architecture restricted to full_sentence only, with a per-subject alignment slope.** Dropping the imagined_sentence trials (essentially noise for every subject in our previous analyses) leaves only the 3874 full_sentence observations. With $\text{Block}_i \equiv 1$ for every trial, the Block-related terms ($b_B, b_{BT}, b_{BS}, b_{BST}, b_{BO}, b_{BOT}$) drop out. The new piece is a per-subject slope $\beta_{s[i]}$ on $R_i = $ `sim_to_target`, which sign-preservingly measures alignment with the true target waveform. The sign of $\beta_s$ tells us whether subject $s$ is aligned ($+$), noise ($\approx 0$), or anti-aligned ($-$, i.e. capable but flipped the class labels).

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{said\_target}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_{\text{obs},i}) \\
p_{\text{obs},i} &= (1 - p_{\text{lapse}}) \cdot \Phi\bigl(\,c_{s[i]} + d_{s[i]} \cdot T_i + \beta_{s[i]} \cdot R_i \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad + b_{ST} \cdot \text{Site}_i \cdot T_i + b_{OT} \cdot \text{Order}_i \cdot T_i \\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad + b_{S} \cdot \text{Site}_i + b_{O} \cdot \text{Order}_i\,\bigr) + p_{\text{lapse}} \cdot 0.5 \\[3pt]
c_{s} &\sim \text{Normal}(\bar c, \sigma_c) \\
d_{s} &\sim \text{Normal}(\bar d, \sigma_d) \\
\beta_{s} &\sim \text{Normal}(\bar\beta, \sigma_\beta) \\
\bar c, \bar d &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5) \\
\bar\beta &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 5) \\
b_{ST}, b_{OT}, b_{S}, b_{O} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.3) \\
\sigma_c, \sigma_d &\sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
\sigma_\beta &\sim \text{Exponential}(0.2) \\
p_{\text{lapse}} &\sim \text{Beta}(2, 20)
\end{aligned}
$$

$\bar\beta$'s prior is wider than the $d'$-shift priors because $R_i$ lives on the raw centered-Pearson-r scale (typical magnitude $\sim 0.04$), so the slope itself can be much larger in absolute units.

**Model 5 (`m5_mix`): M4 + 3-component mirror-constrained mixture prior on $(d_s, \beta_s)$.** Same trial-level likelihood and same 3874 full_sentence observations as M4. The only difference is that the per-subject random effects $(d_s, \beta_s)$, instead of being independent Normals as in M4, are drawn from a three-component bivariate mixture with mirror-constrained means.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{said\_target}_i &\sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_{\text{obs},i}) \\
p_{\text{obs},i} &= (1 - p_{\text{lapse}}) \cdot \Phi(\text{linear predictor as in M4}) + p_{\text{lapse}} \cdot 0.5 \\[6pt]
z_s &\sim \text{Categorical}(\pi_{\text{noise}}, \pi_{\text{correct}}, \pi_{\text{flipped}}) \\
(d_s, \beta_s) \mid z_s {=} \text{noise}   &\sim \mathcal{N}\bigl((0, 0),\ \text{diag}(\sigma_{d,\text{noise}}^2, \sigma_{\beta,\text{noise}}^2)\bigr) \\
(d_s, \beta_s) \mid z_s {=} \text{correct} &\sim \mathcal{N}\bigl((+\mu_d, +\mu_\beta),\ \text{diag}(\sigma_{d,\text{sig}}^2, \sigma_{\beta,\text{sig}}^2)\bigr) \\
(d_s, \beta_s) \mid z_s {=} \text{flipped} &\sim \mathcal{N}\bigl((-\mu_d, -\mu_\beta),\ \text{diag}(\sigma_{d,\text{sig}}^2, \sigma_{\beta,\text{sig}}^2)\bigr) \\[6pt]
\boldsymbol\pi &\sim \text{Dirichlet}([2, 3, 1.5]) \\
\mu_d &\sim \text{Normal}(0.15, 0.15),\ \mu_d > 0 \\
\mu_\beta &\sim \text{Normal}(2, 3),\ \mu_\beta > 0 \\
\sigma_{d,\text{sig}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(5),\quad \sigma_{\beta,\text{sig}} \sim \text{Exponential}(0.5) \\
\sigma_{d,\text{noise}} &\sim \text{Exponential}(10),\quad \sigma_{\beta,\text{noise}} \sim \text{Exponential}(2) \\
c_s &\sim \text{Normal}(\bar c, \sigma_c),\ \ \bar c \sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5),\ \ \sigma_c \sim \text{Exponential}(1) \\
b_{ST}, b_{OT}, b_{S}, b_{O} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.3) \\
p_{\text{lapse}} &\sim \text{Beta}(2, 20)
\end{aligned}
$$

The mirror constraint (the correct and flipped class means are negatives of each other, sharing the same within-class covariance) is what makes the three-component mixture identifiable at our sample size of $n=26$. The latent class $z_s$ is marginalized in the likelihood, so per-subject $P(z_s = k \mid \text{data})$ falls out as a derived quantity in the `generated quantities` block. The question being asked: does the data prefer a discrete three-class structure (noise, correct, flipped) over continuous Normal partial pooling? The funny thing about this hypothesis is that, depending on parameter values, these very different data-generation stories can both produce roughly Gaussian-looking per-subject distributions of $d_s$ and $\beta_s$. This approach is meant to ask whether that Gaussian-looking data is coming from three discrete clusters or just one continuous spread. I wanted to do a Fourier-esque approach but don't have time and it has its own complications.

**What differs across models.**

- **M1 $\to$ M2**: change DV from `correct` to `said_target`, change link from logit to probit, and reparameterize so that the slope on $T_i$ IS the population $d'$. The Block $\times$ TrueTarget interaction $b_{BT}$ in M2 is a cleaner test of "does full_sentence raise sensitivity" than the Block main effect $bB\_bar$ in M1, because it separates sensitivity from criterion. M2 also explicitly tracks Block $\times$ Site and Block $\times$ Order shifts on BOTH $d'$ AND criterion via the dedicated interaction terms.
- **M2 $\to$ M3**: add the lapse mixture. If subjects lapse meaningfully, $\bar d$ should rise in M3 because lapse-induced 50/50 noise is now absorbed by $p_{\text{lapse}}$ rather than dragging the engaged-trial $d'$ toward zero. In practice this depends on whether per-subject performance is far enough from chance for lapse trials to be distinguishable from real misses (given accuracy $\sim 0.52$ i would guess it wont have much effect).
- **M3 $\to$ M4**: restrict to full_sentence trials (3874 of the original 7748), drop all Block-related terms (since Block is constant), and add a per-subject slope $\beta_s$ on $R_i$ = `sim_to_target`. The flip hypothesis can now be read directly off $\beta_s$: negative = anti-aligned with target, consistent with label-flipping; near zero = noise; positive = correctly aligned. No manual flip operation anywhere.
- **M4 $\to$ M5**: linear predictor, observations, lapse, and covariate-shift terms all stay identical. The only difference is that the per-subject random effects $(d_s, \beta_s)$ come from a mirror-constrained three-component mixture instead of independent Normals. M5 fit in `cmdstanr` directly rather than via `ulam` because the discrete latent class $z_s$ has to be marginalized out by hand. M4-vs-M5 WAIC compare answers: "does the discrete class structure (noise / correct / flipped) win over continuous heterogeneity, or does a single continuous normal capture everything?".

**Prior choices.**

The location priors on $\bar c$ and $\bar d$ are $\text{Normal}(0, 0.5)$ so that they are centered on unbiased / chance, with $\sim 95\%$ prior mass within $\pm 1$ on the probit scale (which corresponds to mild bias up to $\sim 16\%/84\%$ response rates on the criterion side, and $d'$ within $\pm 1$ on the sensitivity side). The NHT approach gave the largest result Oberlin full sentence at $d' = 0.137$, so $\pm 1$ is plenty wide without baking direction in. Interaction and main-effect coefficients ($b_{BT}, b_{ST}, b_{OT}, b_{BST}, b_{BOT}, b_{B}, b_{S}, b_{O}, b_{BS}, b_{BO}$) get tighter $\text{Normal}(0, 0.3)$ priors to reflect that shifts in $d'$ or criterion across conditions should be smaller in magnitude than the population-level means themselves.

$p_{\text{lapse}} \sim \text{Beta}(2, 20)$ matches the HW4 prior: prior mean $\sim 0.09$ with most mass below $0.25$, encoding "subjects mostly try, but some non-trivial fraction of trials may be lapses."

M1 uses slightly different priors because it's on the log-odds scale rather than the probit: $a\_bar \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1.5)$ is the standard weakly-informative log-odds intercept ($\sim 95\%$ prior mass corresponds to probabilities in $[0.05, 0.95]$); $bB\_bar, bSite, bOrder \sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.5)$ for main effects; $bB\_site, bB\_order \sim \text{Normal}(0, 0.3)$ tighter for interactions. Per-subject SDs $\sigma_a, \sigma_{bB} \sim \text{Exponential}(1)$.

For M4 and M5 the new alignment parameter $\bar\beta$ gets a much wider prior $\text{Normal}(0, 5)$ because $R_i$ = `sim_to_target` is on the raw centered-Pearson-r scale, with typical magnitude $\sim 0.04$. Correspondingly $\sigma_\beta \sim \text{Exponential}(0.2)$ allows substantial between-subject heterogeneity on alignment.

The M5 mixture priors are weakly informative but locate the correct class somewhere reasonable: $\mu_d \sim \text{Normal}(0.15, 0.15)$ truncated to positive centers the correct-class mean d$'$ near the previously-reported Oberlin-full d$'$ from the NHT, and $\mu_\beta \sim \text{Normal}(2, 3)$ truncated to positive places the correct-class alignment in the same ballpark as $\bar\beta$ in M4. The within-class SDs are intentionally tight on the noise class ($\sigma_{d,\text{noise}} \sim \text{Exp}(10)$, $\sigma_{\beta,\text{noise}} \sim \text{Exp}(2)$ since this hypothesis suggests that the noise class should be a tight blob near the origin) and looser on the signal classes ($\sigma_{d,\text{sig}} \sim \text{Exp}(5)$, $\sigma_{\beta,\text{sig}} \sim \text{Exp}(0.5)$). The Dirichlet$([2, 3, 1.5])$ on $\boldsymbol\pi$ encodes mild prior preference for $\pi_{\text{correct}} > \pi_{\text{noise}} > \pi_{\text{flipped}}$ without being so informative that the data couldn't override it. The mirror constraint (the correct and flipped class means are exact negatives) is hard-coded into the model rather than enforced via prior. I may change this at some later pointbut for now I think it is fine.

____________________________

## 2D. Prior predictive simulation

**Run prior predictive simulations using your assigned priors, but with no real data.**

```{r prior-predictive}
# ============================================================================
# Prior predictive simulation for M3 architecture (SDT + lapse priors).
# M4 adds beta_bar/sigma_beta on top of these and M5 adds mixture-class priors
# (mu_d, mu_beta, pi, etc.). I'm not simulating separately here since
# the probit + lapse + d' machinery is identical and the using this as a sanity
# check to ensure that these priors are expressive enough such that it can actually
# capture the values we saw in previous analyses. 
#
# sample directly from each prior, then push those samples through
# the model equations to see what the priors imply before seeing the data.
# ============================================================================
set.seed(2027)
N_sim <- 4000

# Draw from the priors directly.
# Each line is one prior, sampled N_sim times
c_bar       <- rnorm(N_sim, 0, 0.5)   # population criterion
d_bar       <- rnorm(N_sim, 0, 0.5)   # population d'
sigma_c     <- rexp(N_sim, 1)         # between-subject criterion SD
sigma_d     <- rexp(N_sim, 1)         # between-subject d' SD
beta_BT     <- rnorm(N_sim, 0, 0.3)   # Block-induced d' shift
beta_ST     <- rnorm(N_sim, 0, 0.3)   # Site-induced d' shift
p_lapse     <- rbeta(N_sim, 2, 20)    # lapse rate

# Run the data through the models
# imagined uchicago (d_imag_UC) is the reference
# the others add the relevant shift terms.
d_imag_UC <- d_bar
d_full_UC <- d_bar + beta_BT
d_imag_Ob <- d_bar + beta_ST
d_full_Ob <- d_bar + beta_BT + beta_ST

# synthetic hit and FA rates in the reference cell (imagined/UChicago) in the mixture model
#   - T = +0.5 for target trials
#   - T = -0.5 for distractor trials
#   - H_eng = engaged-state hit rate 
#   - F_eng = engaged-state false alarm rate 
#   - H_obs = observed hit rate after mixing in lapses
#   - F_obs = observed false alarm rate after mixing in lapses
H_eng <- pnorm(c_bar + d_bar * 0.5)
F_eng <- pnorm(c_bar + d_bar * -0.5)
H_obs <- (1 - p_lapse) * H_eng + p_lapse * 0.5
F_obs <- (1 - p_lapse) * F_eng + p_lapse * 0.5
acc_obs <- 0.5 * H_obs + 0.5 * (1 - F_obs)   # if trials are 50/50

# Implied subject-level d's across 1000 draws of (d_bar, sigma_d)
# For each prior draw, simulate 26 subjects, then pool them
n_subj <- 26
n_draws <- 1000

sim_subj <- tibble(
  draw = rep(1:n_draws, each = n_subj),
  d = rnorm(n_draws * n_subj,
            mean = rep(d_bar[1:n_draws], each = n_subj),
            sd   = rep(sigma_d[1:n_draws], each = n_subj))
)

# Three draws of 26 subjects each plotted independently
# ot get a sense of what some draws of 26 CAN look like given these priors
sim_subj_d_1 <- rnorm(n_subj, d_bar[1], sigma_d[1])
sim_subj_d_2 <- rnorm(n_subj, d_bar[1], sigma_d[1])
sim_subj_d_3 <- rnorm(n_subj, d_bar[1], sigma_d[1])

```

**Visualize these simulations (using one or a few plots) to assess their reasonableness**

```{r prior-predictive-viz}
# Plot 1
# =============================================================
# per-cell d'. Centered on 0 with most data in +/- 1.
prior_d_long <- tibble(

)

# =============================================================


# Plot 3

# implied subject-level d' for 1000 (d_bar, sigma_d) draws

p_prior_subj_1 <- ggplot(sim_subj_1, aes(x = d)) +

       subtitle = "26 synthetic subjects from one (d_bar, sigma_d) draw",

sim_subj_2 <- tibble(subj = 1:n_subj, d = sim_subj_d_2)
p_prior_subj_2 <- ggplot(sim_subj_2, aes(x = d)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "maroon", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Prior predictive: implied subject-level d' #2",
       subtitle = "26 synthetic subjects from one (d_bar, sigma_d) draw",
       x = "Subject d'", y = "Number of synthetic subjects")

sim_subj_3 <- tibble(subj = 1:n_subj, d = sim_subj_d_3)
p_prior_subj_3 <- ggplot(sim_subj_3, aes(x = d)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "maroon", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +

       subtitle = "26 synthetic subjects from one (d_bar, sigma_d) draw",
       x = "Subject d'", y = "Number of synthetic subjects")

plot_grid(p_prior_d, p_prior_acc, p_prior_subj, p_prior_subj_1, p_prior_subj_2, p_prior_subj_3, ncol = 2)
```

**Are your priors distributed in a way that makes sense and leads to a sensible range of parameter values?**

____________________________

Yes things make sense here.

1 - Per cell prior on $d'$ is centered on 0 with most mass within $\pm 1$. Our earlier analyses showed Oberlin full at $d' = 0.137$ the priors are wide enough to accommodate the empirical signal without baking direction in. 

2 - After adding the lapse mixture we can see that the observed accuracy in the reference cell peaks near 0.5 with very little mass outside $[0.35, 0.65]$ which mostly seems to reflect that most subjects in this paradigm hover near chance. Since above chance performance is typically close to 0.5, I don't expect the lapse term to have too much effect (like its effect on congruent vs incongruent trials in HW4).

3/4 - Looking at both the pooled histogram (Plot 3) and the individual draws of 26 subjects (Plot 4), the priors imply reasonable between-subject variability. The pooled distribution is centered near 0 and mostly lies within about [-2, 2], indicating that extreme subject-level d' values are possible but uncommon.

## 2E. Your data and experimental procedure

**Please write out details regarding your participants and the specifics of your experimental design, including:**

- Specify the number of participants in your study.

- Specify relevant sample descriptive details regarding e.g., age ranges, education levels, species type, etc.

- Describe your dependent variable(s) of interest.

- Describe your independent variables.

*If your data are experimental:*
- List the number of trials per condition in your experiment.
- Describe the procedures of your experiment.

____________________________

**Participants.** 26 native-English-speaking undergraduates (age range roughly 18–25): 16 at Oberlin, 10 at UChicago. UChicago data was collected by Arwen Bare for her senior honors thesis (Bare, 2025) under Dr. Howard Nusbaum's advising. Oberlin data was collected independently by Connor Daley at Oberlin. All participants gave written informed consent. The protocol was approved by the University of Chicago IRB (#24-1770). UChicago subjects were offered 1.5 course credits plus a raffle entry for a $50 gift card tied to performance. Oberlin recruitment was administered separately. We excluded one subject from Oberlin due to a technical issue resulting in their inability to complete the study. We also excluded a single subject from the University of Chicago as a trial-by-trial look at their data revelead they only pressed a single key for the entire experiment.

**Stimuli.** The target signal is the word *wall*, extracted from a clean recording of the carrier sentence "The picture hung on the wall" produced by a male native-English-speaking speaker with a midwestern accent (age 55) in a sound-isolation booth (Bare, 2025). The full sentence was recorded with a studio-quality condenser microphone at 44.1 kHz / 16-bit stereo, converted to mono, downsampled to 8 kHz, and amplitude-normalized; the final word *wall* was segmented out as a 360 ms / 8 kHz / 16-bit mono clip to serve as the correlation template. The noise stimuli were generated from quantum-random seeds fetched from the ANU Quantum Random Number Generator, expanded via the ChaCha20 stream cipher into approximately 2.8 million candidate 360 ms white-noise clips at 8 kHz / 16-bit mono. Each candidate was scored by Pearson correlation against the *wall* template; the 153 highest-correlation clips became the labeled "targets" ($r \in [0.072, 0.090]$) and the 153 lowest-$|r|$ clips became the "distractors" ($|r| < 1.5 \times 10^{-6}$). 6 clips (3 target, 3 distractor) were held out for instruction examples, and the remainder were split into the two experimental blocks. Stimuli were RMS-normalized to –23 dBFS for presentation. Since Pearson $r$ is invariant to positive linear scaling, this normalization does not change the target/distractor correlation structure.

**Dependent variables.** M1's DV is `correct` $\in \{0,1\}$ (subject's response matches the experimenter's label). M2-M5's DV is `said_target` $\in \{0,1\}$ (the subject's raw response, regardless of the experimenter's label). In the SDT formulation, `said_target` plus `true_target` jointly give us hits and false alarms, which give us $d'$ via the slope on `true_target_centered`. The reason we prefer the SDT version: $d'$ separates sensitivity (the thing the experiment is trying to measure) from criterion (response bias, a nuisance), and the per-subject d-prime numbers can be read directly against the Bayesian estimates (as explained earlier).

**Independent variables.**

- **Block** (within-subject, 2 levels: `imagined_sentence`, `full_sentence`). In `imagined_sentence` the subject imagines the beginning of the carrier phrase "The picture hung on the" silently before clicking to play each trial's noise clip (and is instructed not to subvocalize the phrase); in `full_sentence` they hear the beginning of the carrier phrase "The picture hung on the" in the original speaker's voice immediately before each noise clip plays.
- **Site** (between-subject, 2 levels: `UChicago`, `Oberlin`). Observational.
- **BlockOrder** (between-subject, 2 levels: full sentence is either first or second). Counterbalanced.
- **TrueTarget** (trial-level, $\in \{-0.5, +0.5\}$ centered). The experimenter's label for the stimulus, determined by Pearson-r against the "wall" template. Randomized within each 149-trial block.

**Number of trials per condition.** Each subject runs 149 trials × 2 blocks = 298 trials. Total trials in the dataset: $26 \times 298 = 7{,}748$. Within each block, target/distractor labels are roughly balanced (75/74 or 74/75).

**Procedure.** Subjects ran the task in person in a quiet room with Sennheiser HD-280 headphones (Bare, 2025). They were instructed that on each trial they would hear a sound and would need to indicate whether the word *wall* was present (key 'y' for Yes, key 'n' for No), and they were given 6 example stimuli (3 target, 3 distractor) to familiarize themselves with the task before any experimental trials. They could replay these as many times as they wished and could also re-listen to the clean *wall* template and the full carrier sentence. The two blocks ran in counterbalanced order with a 5-minute break between them; the Stanford Sleepiness Scale was administered at the start of each block. Within each block, "refresher" periods every 15 trials replayed the full carrier sentence "The picture hung on the wall" five times to keep the prior active. No trial time limits were imposed and no per-trial feedback was given. The full session lasted 60–90 minutes including post-task questionnaires.

A battery of pre/post-block questionnaires was collected: the Tellegen Absorption Scale (TAS; Tellegen & Atkinson, 1974), the Voice Hearing Questionnaire (VHQ; Posey & Losch, 1983), the Dissociative Experiences Scale II (DES-II), the Bucknell Auditory Imagery Scale (BAIS; vividness and control subscales), the Launay-Slade Hallucination Scale (LSHS; Launay & Slade, 1981), the Flow State Scale (9-item version), and the Stanford Sleepiness Scale. These were important for our original hypothesis that hallucination-proneness traits predict $d'$. The present project does not condition on them because our primary analysis found no questionnaire correlation surviving Bonferroni correction across a 24-test matrix, and the strongest single questionnaire result (an Oberlin full-sentence-block $d'$ × DES-II correlation at $p = 0.079$) wouldn't survive without correction. As a result, for this Bayesian analysis I have decided to leave questionnaires out of the model and focus on the within-subject Block × TrueTarget interaction plus the additional analyses targeting the flip hypothesis (M4, M5).

Make a few (2-3) plots that will help you to interpret your data and your statistical model. This could involve bar plots, scatter plots, box plots, histograms, line graphs, etc.

```{r data-viz, fig.height = 35}
# ============================================================================

# ============================================================================

# Plot 1

# per (subject, block) d' scatter plot that is sectioned by experimental site
p_v1 <- ggplot(subj_block_dprime, aes(x = block_scheme, y = dprime, color = site)) +

  facet_wrap(~ site) +

       x = "Block", y = "Classical d'")
# ============================================================================


# Plot 2
# ============================================================================
# within-subject paired lines, Full Sentence (left) --> Imagined Sentence (Right)
# First step is reshaping the long subj_block_dprime (one row per (subj, block))
# into wide format (one row per subject, with separate columns for each block).
# pivot_wider() does this & names_from() says which column's values become the new
# column names, values_from() says which column fills the new cells.
# Plot 2
# ============================================================================
# Within-subject paired lines going Imagined Sentence (left) -> Full Sentence (right)

# Reshape to wide (one row per subject)
paired_d <- subj_block_dprime |>
  select(site, subject, block_scheme, dprime) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = block_scheme, values_from = dprime)

# Compute mean per site (so each facet gets its own average slope)
mean_line <- paired_d |>
  group_by(site) |>
  summarize(
    imagined_mean = mean(imagined_sentence, na.rm = TRUE),
    full_mean     = mean(full_sentence, na.rm = TRUE),

  )

p_v2 <- ggplot() +

  # endpoints (points)
  geom_point(data = subj_block_dprime,

  # mean slope per site (thicker, black)
  geom_segment(data = mean_line,
               aes(x = "imagined_sentence", xend = "full_sentence",

  facet_wrap(~ site) +

  labs(title = "Within-subject paired d' (Imagined -> Full)",

       x = "Block", y = "Subject d'")
# ============================================================================
# ============================================================================


# Plot 3
# ============================================================================
# pooled per-subject d' with negative-pooled-d' subjects colored red.
# These are the subjects the flip hypothesis is asking about --- whether
# their negative d' is sampling noise or capable-but-flipped responding.
# In the new M4/M5 framework we do not pre-flip them; instead M4's per-subject
# beta_s[s] surfaces the sign, and M5's mixture model assigns each subject
# a posterior P(z_s = flipped).
# We just attach a label column to subj_dprime so we can color by it.
subj_dprime$flip_label <- ifelse(subj_dprime$flip_subject == 1,
                                 "neg pooled d'", "pos pooled d'")
p_v3 <- ggplot(subj_dprime,
               aes(x = reorder(subject, dprime_pooled),     # sort bars by d'
                   y = dprime_pooled, fill = flip_label)) +

# ============================================================================

# Plot 4
# ============================================================================
# per (subject, block) hit rate vs false alarm rate scatter
# This is the underlying SDT geometry that produces d'. Subjects on the
# diagonal (HR = FAR) have d' = 0; subjects above the diagonal have d' > 0
# (correctly discriminating); subjects below the diagonal have d' < 0
# (anti-aligned with the experimenter's labels --- the flip hypothesis).
p_v4 <- ggplot(subj_block_dprime, aes(x = fa_rate, y = hit_rate, color = site)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, alpha = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ block_scheme) +

  labs(title = "Hit rate vs false-alarm rate by block",

       x = "False alarm rate", y = "Hit rate")
# ============================================================================


# Plot 5
# ============================================================================
# per-subject pooled d' histogram, colored by site
# Shows the marginal distribution of subject-level d' across all subjects,
# which is what the M5 mixture is trying to decompose into noise / correct /
# flipped components.
p_v5 <- ggplot(subj_dprime, aes(x = dprime_pooled, fill = site)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 15, alpha = 0.7, position = "identity", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of pooled per-subject d'",
       subtitle = "Red line = 0 (chance). M5 mixture asks whether this is one Normal blob or three clusters.",
       x = "Pooled d'", y = "Subjects")
# ============================================================================

# Plot everythang
plot_grid(p_v1, p_v2, p_v3, p_v4, p_v5, ncol = 1)

```

**Explain what information the plot(s) provide.**

____________________________

Plot 1 shows the per (subject, block) $d'$ with a chance line at 0 and the cell mean as a black crossbar. You can see that Oberlin full_sentence cell is visibly above zero, with 13 out of 16 Oberlin subjects' $d'$ values above the chance line. The other three cells (UChicago full, UChicago imagined, Oberlin imagined) hover around zero with subjects largely symmetric on both sides.

Plot 2 is the within-subject Imagined Sentence to Full Sentence slopes for each subject within in each site. This is what the multilevel $\beta_{BT}$ slope is going to estimate in a (hopefully) more informative way. The average slope across subjects is negative (full to imagined) in both sites but the spread of individual slopes is wide so some subjects slope downward (the manipulation hurt them) and some sharply upward. This is where partial pooling will help. A single population slope $\bar{\beta_{BT}}$ understates the variability, and $\sigma_{\beta_{BT}}$ is needed to quantify it.

Plot 3 is the pooled across-blocks $d'$ per subject, with the negative-pooled-$d'$ subjects (raw pooled $d' < 0$) colored red. These are, to some extent, the subjects the flip hypothesis is asking about. If those red bars are real signal (substantially negative, big magnitude), the per-subject `beta_s` in M4 should come out negative for them and M5's mixture should assign them appreciable posterior mass in the flipped class. If they're just at-chance noise (near zero), both `beta_s` and `P(z_s = flipped)` should sit near zero for them. M5's `pi_flipped` posterior is the population-level answer to "are any subjects credibly flipped? Although we actually intend to use the full sentence block instead of block-pooled, this graph gives one a better sense of the type of transformations we are going to try to apply in a more technical manner via the M4 and M5 analyses.

Plot 4 is the hit rate vs false-alarm rate scatter per (subject, block), with a red dashed line on the chance diagonal. This is the geometry that produces $d'$: a subject sitting on the diagonal has hit rate equal to false-alarm rate so $d' = 0$, a subject above the diagonal has $d' > 0$ (correctly discriminating), and a subject below the diagonal has $d' < 0$ (anti-aligned with the experimenter's labels which is the pattern we are testing under the flip hypothesis). Most subjects in the full_sentence facet sit slightly above the diagonal; the imagined_sentence facet shows subjects more evenly scattered around it. Subjects sitting clearly below the diagonal in either facet are the ones M4's per-subject $\beta_s$ and M5's flipped class are trying to pick out.

Plot 5 is the histogram of pooled per-subject $d'$ colored by site. This is the marginal distribution that M5's mixture is trying to decompose: the question M5 asks is whether this distribution is better described as one Normal blob (continuous heterogeneity around a single population mean) or as three discrete clusters (a noise cluster at 0, a correct cluster at $+\mu$, and a flipped cluster at $-\mu$). At $n = 26$ a histogram this small is consistent with both stories visually. There is a concern that given the correct population proportions (most people are at chance, and correct/correct-but-flipped are equally likely) then the data generated by both hypotheses would be identical! However it is unlikely that the latter hypothesis would produce exactly a gaussian, so we will have to see if n = 26 is enough data to really test between these hypotheses.

____________________________

**Explain whether the plot(s) offer you any information regarding your effects of interest and what your anticipated results might be.**

____________________________

- **Population $\bar d$ in the reference cell (imagined/UC/first)**: very close to 0, narrow credible interval. The reference cell is just at chance.
- **Block × TrueTarget interaction $\beta_{BT}$**: modestly positive. Credible interval will likely straddle 0 narrowly but with most posterior mass above 0. Bigger in Oberlin than in UChicago.
- **Site × TrueTarget interaction $\beta_{ST}$**: positive (Oberlin > UChicago in $d'$), credible interval probably includes 0 given the small site samples but with most mass above 0.
- **Order × TrueTarget $\beta_{OT}$**: near 0 across the board, with one possible exception. Our previous analysese found a trend in the Oberlin imagined block where second-block subjects had higher $d'$ than first-block ($d=1.03$, $p=0.078$). With $n_{B2}=5$ which is certainly a fragile result, but the multilevel framework will give us an interval for it.
- **$\sigma_d$**: non-trivially above 0 which is consistent with the spread we see in Plot 1.
- **$p_\text{lapse}$ (M3)**: probably small, in the 0.05–0.20 range. With 7,748 trials there's plenty of data to estimate this. However, even the best performers had accuracies <0.6 so at a 50% guess rate there is only so much needle that this parameter could move.
- **M4/M5 ($\bar\beta$, $\sigma_\beta$, per-subject $\beta_s$)**: $\bar\beta$ should be cleanly positive if subjects on average track per-trial r (which the convergent evidence from our original analysis suggests). Per-subject $\beta_s$ is the interesting one Although not present in these plots, the idea is to give a clearer visual about the type of thing that we are going to do. Subjects with negative $d'$ should sit at $\beta_s$ near zero if they're noise, or substantially negative if they're capable-but-flipped. If a couple of negative-$d'$ subjects come out with credibly-negative $\beta_s$ that's first-pass evidence for the flip hypothesis. Once again that is not exactly what this graph shows, but this is just meant to give a flavor of the two hypotheses that we are testing.
- **Hit/FA geometry (Plot 4)**: most subjects in full_sentence sit slightly above the chance diagonal which is consistent with a modestly positive $\beta_{BT}$ and a small positive $\beta_{ST}$. The subjects sitting clearly below the diagonal are the ones M4's per-subject $\beta_s$ should flag with negative posterior mass; if those subjects line up with the red bars from Plot 3, that's convergent first-pass evidence for the flip-hypothesis subpopulation that M5 is trying to estimate via $\pi_\text{flipped}$.
- **Marginal d' distribution (Plot 5)**: with only 26 subjects, the histogram is too coarse to visually distinguish "one Normal blob" from "three discrete clusters at $-\mu$, $0$, $+\mu$." This is exactly the ambiguity the WAIC compare between M4 (continuous Normal partial pooling) and M5 (mixture prior) is designed to resolve. It will be hard to interpret these results given the limited data, but we will see.
