# 3. Results

## 3A. Fit your models

**Fit your statistical models using ulam.**

```{r fit-m1-acc, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)

# ============================================================================
# M1 Section
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# multilevel logistic on accuracy
# Varying intercept per subject (a[s]) and varying Block slope per subject
# (bB[s]). Between-subject predictors (site, order) get fixed slopes.
# Block x Site and Block x Order interactions added so we can see whether
# the Block effect is concentrated in one site or one order condition.
future_1 <- future({m1_acc <- ulam(
  alist(
    
    # Estimate accuracy via binomial distribution
    correct ~ dbinom(1, p),
    
    # logit link to cast into probability valued results
    logit(p) <- 
      
      # per-subject baseline log-odds of being correct in the reference cell
      # (imagined / UChicago / first block) and partial pooled toward a_bar
      a[subject_idx] +
      
      # within-subject effect of block
      # per-subject Block slope
      # how much full_sentence shifts log-odds of being correct relative to imagined_sentence
      bB[subject_idx] * block +
      
      # between-subject main effects
      # site main effect (Oberlin = 1, UChicago = 0). This is observational so wont treat this as causal!!
      bSite  * site +
      
      # order main effect (2nd block = 1, 1st block = 0). Captures any
      # practice / fatigue across the two blocks 
      # (vaguely measured by stanford sleepines questionnaire but tbh never understood that one)
      bOrder * order +
      
      # INTERACTIONS
      # Block x Site: does the Block bump look different at the two sites?
      bB_site * block * site +
      
      # Block x Order: is the Block bump bigger when full comes 1st vs 2nd?
      bB_order * block * order, 

    # Varying parameters per subject
    # per-subject intercept lives as a Gaussian around grand mean a_bar with
    # between-subject SD sigma_a
    a[subject_idx]  ~ dnorm(a_bar, sigma_a),
    
    # per-subject Block slope lives in a Gaussian around bB_bar w/ SD sigma_bB
    bB[subject_idx] ~ dnorm(bB_bar, sigma_bB),

    # Population-level priors
    # wide prior on grand-mean log-odds; 1.5 SD covers ~0.05-0.95 on prob scale
    a_bar    ~ dnorm(0, 1.5),
    
    # tighter prior on the population Block effect since we, empirically, dont expect a huge log-odds shift from this manipulation
    bB_bar   ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    
    # interaction priors tighter still (barring particular circumstances it seems
    # that interactions are usually smaller than main effects...
    #   so we want to regularize them harder)
    bB_site  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bB_order ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    
    # exponential priors on the between-subject SDs
    sigma_a  ~ dexp(1),
    sigma_bB ~ dexp(1),

    # Fixed effects
    # site and order each get a moderate prior
    bSite    ~ dnorm(0,   0.5),
    bOrder   ~ dnorm(0,   0.5)
  ),
  data    = slim,
  warmup  = 1500,
  iter    = 5000,
  refresh = 0,
  chains  = chains_to_use,
  cores   = cores_to_use,
  # save log_lik so we can do WAIC / PSIS later 
  # the hatred i have for the implementation of log lik...
  # makes it impossible to do within-chain threading!!!!!!
  # I have great respect for McElreath but whyyyy is the single most important
  # function in the package built such that there is NO ADVANTAGE (!!??!?!?!?)
  # WHATSOEVER FOR HAVING MORE CORES THAN CHAINS?!?!?! WHy would you kneecap your
  # users like this. To be fair  I will admit  that the underlying challenges are tricky and I get it! 
  # It is doable but a rea pain in the rearend.....
  # But good lord I need people to know that there is no reason this code takes as long as it does
  log_lik = TRUE,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)
)})
```

```{r fit-m2-sdt, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)
# ============================================================================
# M2 Section
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# multilevel signal detection theory (d'). DV is said_target.
# Slope on true_target is d' (probit link + true_target centered to +/-0.5
# which makes the slope Gaussian d' which is a neat little trick!)
#
# Per-subject c[s] (criterion) and d[s] (sensitivity) as parameters.
# Block, Site, Order each get a criterion-shift (bB, bS, bO) AND a d'-shift
# (bBT, bST, bOT). Block x Site and Block x Order get both a criterion-shift
# interaction (bBS, bBO) and a d'-shift interaction (bBST, bBOT). bBST is
# the Oberlin x full_sentence d' (the result that I want to get a bayesian perspective on)
future_2 <- future({m2_sdt <- ulam(
  alist(
    
    # Bernoulli trial-level likelihood on the subject's raw response
    said_target ~ dbinom(1, p),
    
    # probit link
    # Phi() is the std normal CDF. Combined with true_target centered at +/-0.5
    # the slope on true_target IS classical Gaussian d'
    p <- Phi(
      
      # per-subject criterion (intercept in probit space)
      # response bias for the reference cell, partial pooled toward c_bar
      c[subject_idx] +
      
      # per-subject sensitivity (d')
      # this is the headline parameter of this entire analysis
      d[subject_idx] * true_target +
      
      # D'-SHIFT INTERACTIONS (sensitivity shifts across conditions)
      # Block x TrueTarget: full_sentence vs imagined_sentence d' shift
      bBT  * block * true_target +
      
      # Site x TrueTarget: Oberlin vs UChicago d' shift (observational!)
      bST  * site  * true_target +
      
      # Order x TrueTarget: 2nd-block vs 1st-block d' shift (practice effect)
      bOT  * order * true_target +
      
      # Block x Site x TrueTarget: the headline three-way interaction
      # does the full_sentence boost look different at Oberlin vs UChicago?
      bBST * block * site  * true_target +
      
      # Block x Order x TrueTarget: does the full_sentence boost depend on
      # whether full came 1st or 2nd?
      bBOT * block * order * true_target +
      
      # CRITERION SHIFTS (response bias shifts, NOT sensitivity)
      # Block main effect on criterion
      bB  * block +
      
      # Site main effect on criterion
      bS  * site  +
      
      # Order main effect on criterion
      bO  * order +
      
      # Block x Site criterion interaction
      bBS * block * site +
      
      # Block x Order criterion interaction
      bBO * block * order
    ),
    
    # Varying parameters per subject
    # per-subject criterion lives in a Gaussian around c_bar with SD sigma_c
    c[subject_idx] ~ dnorm(c_bar, sigma_c),
    
    # per-subject sensitivity lives in a Gaussian around d_bar with SD sigma_d
    d[subject_idx] ~ dnorm(d_bar, sigma_d),
    
    # Population-level priors
    # population criterion centered on 0 (unbiased). 0.5 SD allows mild bias
    c_bar ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    
    # population d' centered on 0 (chance). 95% prior mass within +/-1
    # plenty wide for this paradigm (biggest cell from thesis was Oberlin full at 0.137)
    d_bar ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    
    # d'-shift priors (tighter than d_bar; shifts should be smaller than the mean)
    bBT  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bST  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bOT  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBST ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBOT ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    
    # criterion-shift priors (same tightness as d'-shifts)
    bB  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bS  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bO  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBS ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBO ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    
    # exponential priors on the between-subject SDs
    sigma_c ~ dexp(1),
    sigma_d ~ dexp(1)
  ),
  data    = slim,
  refresh = 0,
  warmup  = 1500,
  iter    = 5000,
  chains  = chains_to_use,
  cores   = cores_to_use,
  log_lik = TRUE,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)
)})
```

```{r fit-m3-sdt-mix, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)
# ============================================================================
# M3 Section
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Basically just M2 with the p_lapse mixture model from hw4
future_3 <- future({m3_sdt_mix <- ulam(
  alist(
    
    # likelihood now on p_obs (observed response prob after mixing in lapses)
    said_target ~ dbinom(1, p_obs),
    
    # here is that mixture we all love so much
    # (1 - p_lapse) * Phi(SDT linear pred) for engaged trials
    # plus p_lapse * 0.5 for lapse trials (50/50 guess)
    # Even though subjects saw either 75 targets & 74 distractors or vice versa,
    # taking this does not effect probability of a guess being correct....
    # it only changes the expected counts for target & correct given a guess
    # and distractor & correct given guess
    p_obs <- (1 - p_lapse) * Phi(
      
      # all of this is identical to M2 (same linear predictor)
      c[subject_idx] +
      d[subject_idx] * true_target +
      
      # d'-shift interactions
      bBT  * block * true_target +
      bST  * site  * true_target +
      bOT  * order * true_target +
      bBST * block * site  * true_target +
      bBOT * block * order * true_target +
      
      # criterion shifts
      bB  * block +
      bS  * site  +
      bO  * order +
      bBS * block * site +
      bBO * block * order
    ) + p_lapse * 0.5,
    
    # same partial pooling as M2
    c[subject_idx] ~ dnorm(c_bar, sigma_c),
    d[subject_idx] ~ dnorm(d_bar, sigma_d),
    
    # same population-level priors as M2
    c_bar ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    d_bar ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    
    # d'-shift priors
    bBT  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bST  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bOT  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBST ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBOT ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    
    # criterion-shift priors
    bB  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bS  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bO  ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBS ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bBO ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    
    # between-subject SDs
    sigma_c ~ dexp(1),
    sigma_d ~ dexp(1),
    
    # M2 Beta(2, 20) prior on lapse rate
    # encodes the idea that subjects mostly try but it is a long boring task
    #   (relative i suppose) and people likely loswe attention sometimes
    p_lapse ~ dbeta(2, 20)
  ),
  data    = slim,
  refresh = 0,
  warmup  = 1500,
  iter    = 5000,
  chains  = chains_to_use,
  cores   = cores_to_use,
  log_lik = TRUE,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)
)})
```

```{r fit-m4-full-beta, results = "hide"}
set.seed(2026)

# ============================================================================
# M4 Section (non-centered parameterization)
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Same general structure as M3 but just the full_sentence trials and with
# a per-subject slope on sim_to_target (centered Pearson r).since block
# is constant we drop terms with a `block` factor (i.e bB, bBT, bBS, bBST, bBO, bBOT).
# This leaves us with criterion, d', beta_truetarget, Site/Order shifts on each, and the lapse rate.
#
# how to read beta_s[s]:
#   - beta_s[s] > 0: subject's responses align with per-trial r-to-target (correct labels)
#   - beta_s[s] ~ 0: subject's responses do not track r (noise)
#   - beta_s[s] < 0: subject's responses are anti-aligned with r (signal detection with flipped labels)
#
#
# NON-CENTERED parameterization on c, d, beta_s. With small sigma_d and sigma_beta
# the centered version creates a Neal-style funnel (when sigma is small,
# per-subject d[i] must hug d_bar; when sigma is large d[i] can be anywhere).
# HMC handles that geometry poorly which shows up as low ESS and high rhat on
# d_bar, sigma_d, beta_bar, sigma_beta in the centered fit. Non-centered just
# samples raw N(0, 1) per-subject offsets and applies location/scale deterministically.
#  Credit to claude for hleping me understand exactly why this kept diverging
#    i spent so much time trying and failing to figure this out so very grateful
future_4 <- future({m4_full_beta <- ulam(
  alist(
    
    # Bernoulli likelihood on the raw response (no flipping)
    said_target ~ dbinom(1, p_obs),
    
    # same lapse mixutre from M3
    p_obs <- (1 - p_lapse) * Phi(
      
      # criterion (probit space) - per-subject, reconstructed below
      c[subject_idx] +
      
      # per-subject sensitivity (as measured by d') on the binary target label
      d[subject_idx] * true_target +
      
      # per-subject slope on the continuous per-trial r-to-target
      # this is the sign-preserving alignment metric
      beta_s[subject_idx] * sim_to_target +
      
      # interactions
      # Site x TrueTarget: Oberlin vs UChicago d' shift within full_sentence
      bST * site  * true_target +
      
      # Order x TrueTarget: 2nd-block vs 1st-block d' shift within full_sentence
      bOT * order * true_target +
      
      # Criterion/bias 
      bS * site +
      bO * order
    ) + p_lapse * 0.5,
    
    # NON-CENTERED reconstruction: per-subject params are bar + scale * raw
    # where raw ~ N(0, 1). Deterministic (no priors on these).
    transpars> vector[N_sub]:c      <<- c_bar    + sigma_c    * c_raw,
    transpars> vector[N_sub]:d      <<- d_bar    + sigma_d    * d_raw,
    transpars> vector[N_sub]:beta_s <<- beta_bar + sigma_beta * beta_raw,
    
    # the raws are what HMC actually samples: unit-variance standard normals
    vector[N_sub]:c_raw    ~ dnorm(0, 1),
    vector[N_sub]:d_raw    ~ dnorm(0, 1),
    vector[N_sub]:beta_raw ~ dnorm(0, 1),
    
    # population-level priors as in M3 for c and d
    c_bar    ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    d_bar    ~ dnorm(0, 0.5),
    
    # beta is on a different scale (per-trial r is centered around 0 with magnitude ~0.04)
    # so the slope itself can be much larger in absolute units. wider prior to match.
    beta_bar ~ dnorm(0, 5),
    
    # d'-shift priors
    bST ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bOT ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    
    # criterion-shift priors
    bS ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    bO ~ dnorm(0, 0.3),
    
    # between-subject SDs
    sigma_c    ~ dexp(1),
    sigma_d    ~ dexp(1),
    sigma_beta ~ dexp(0.2),
    
    # lapse prior (same Beta(2, 20) as M3)
    p_lapse ~ dbeta(2, 20)
  ),
  data    = slim_full,
  refresh = 0,
  warmup  = 1500,
  iter    = 5000,
  chains  = chains_to_use,
  cores   = cores_to_use,
  log_lik = TRUE,
  control = list(adapt_delta = 0.99, max_treedepth = 12)
)})
```


```{r fit-m5-mix, results = "hide"}
# ============================================================================
# M5 Section
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Same trial-level likelihood and same 3874 full_sentence observations as M4.
# Only difference: instead of (d_s, beta_s) coming from independent Normals,
# they come from a mirror-constrained 3-component bivariate mixture:
#
#   z_s ~ Categorical(pi_noise, pi_correct, pi_flipped)
#   (d_s, beta_s) | z_s = noise   ~ N2((0, 0),         Sigma_noise)
#   (d_s, beta_s) | z_s = correct ~ N2((+mu_d, +mu_b), Sigma_signal)
#   (d_s, beta_s) | z_s = flipped ~ N2((-mu_d, -mu_b), Sigma_signal)
#
# Mirror constraint (correct/flipped means are negatives of each other) is what
# makes the 3-component mixture (mayyybe) identifiable with only 26 subjects. The latent
# z_s is marginalized in the likelihood. this gives per-subject P(z_s = flipped | data)
# falling out as a derived quantity.
#
# Same observations as M4 so M4 vs M5 WAIC can hopefully give the flip-hypothesis test
# (continuous random effects vs discrete mixture).
#
# Cannot do discrete mixture marginalization cleanly in ulam, so had to drop into
# cmdstanr directly. log_lik is generated for WAIC compare against M4.

# m5_data lives in the main process so that the
# m5-summary chunk below can reference m5_data$S after the fit comes back.
# Everything else (stan code, compile, sample) stays inside the future.
#
m5_data <- list(
  N           = length(slim_full$said_target),
  S           = slim_full$N_sub,
  subj        = slim_full$subject_idx,
  said_target = slim_full$said_target,
  true_target = slim_full$true_target,
  sim         = slim_full$sim_to_target,
  site        = slim_full$site,
  order       = slim_full$order
)

future_5 <- future({m5_stan_code <- "
data {
  int<lower=1> N;
  int<lower=1> S;
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=S> subj;
  array[N] int<lower=0, upper=1> said_target;
  vector[N] true_target;
  vector[N] sim;
  vector[N] site;
  vector[N] order;
}

parameters {
  // Population criterion
  real c_bar;
  real<lower=0> sigma_c;
  vector[S] c_raw;

  // Mixture proportions over (noise, correct, flipped)
  simplex[3] pi;

  // Class means (positive by construction; flipped class is the mirror)
  real<lower=0> mu_d;
  real<lower=0> mu_beta;

  // Within-class SDs (signal classes share; noise has its own)
  real<lower=0> sigma_d_sig;
  real<lower=0> sigma_b_sig;
  real<lower=0> sigma_d_noise;
  real<lower=0> sigma_b_noise;

  // Per-subject d' and beta_truetarget (drawn from the mixture)
  vector[S] d;
  vector[S] beta_s;

  // Covariate shifts (block dropped since full_sentence only)
  real bST; real bOT;
  real bS;  real bO;

  real<lower=0, upper=1> p_lapse;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[S] c = c_bar + sigma_c * c_raw;
}

model {
  // Priors
  c_bar ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  sigma_c ~ exponential(1);
  c_raw ~ std_normal();

  mu_d ~ normal(0.15, 0.15);
  mu_beta ~ normal(2, 3);
  sigma_d_sig ~ exponential(5);
  sigma_b_sig ~ exponential(0.5);
  sigma_d_noise ~ exponential(10);
  sigma_b_noise ~ exponential(2);

  // Mildly downweight flipped class relative to correct
  pi ~ dirichlet([2, 3, 1.5]');

  bST ~ normal(0, 0.3); bOT ~ normal(0, 0.3);
  bS  ~ normal(0, 0.3); bO  ~ normal(0, 0.3);

  p_lapse ~ beta(2, 20);

  // Per-subject (d, beta) ~ marginalized 3-component mixture
  for (s in 1:S) {
    vector[3] log_class;
    log_class[1] = log(pi[1])
                 + normal_lpdf(d[s]      | 0, sigma_d_noise)
                 + normal_lpdf(beta_s[s] | 0, sigma_b_noise);
    log_class[2] = log(pi[2])
                 + normal_lpdf(d[s]      |  mu_d,    sigma_d_sig)
                 + normal_lpdf(beta_s[s] |  mu_beta, sigma_b_sig);
    log_class[3] = log(pi[3])
                 + normal_lpdf(d[s]      | -mu_d,    sigma_d_sig)
                 + normal_lpdf(beta_s[s] | -mu_beta, sigma_b_sig);
    target += log_sum_exp(log_class);
  }

  // Trial likelihood (same SDT + lapse structure as M4)
  for (t in 1:N) {
    real lp = c[subj[t]]
            + d[subj[t]] * true_target[t]
            + beta_s[subj[t]] * sim[t]
            + bST * site[t]  * true_target[t]
            + bOT * order[t] * true_target[t]
            + bS  * site[t]
            + bO  * order[t];
    real p_eng = Phi(lp);
    real p_obs = (1 - p_lapse) * p_eng + p_lapse * 0.5;
    said_target[t] ~ bernoulli(p_obs);
  }
}

generated quantities {
  // Per-subject posterior class probabilities (for inspection)
  matrix[S, 3] p_class;
  vector[N] log_lik;

  for (s in 1:S) {
    vector[3] log_class;
    log_class[1] = log(pi[1])
                 + normal_lpdf(d[s]      | 0, sigma_d_noise)
                 + normal_lpdf(beta_s[s] | 0, sigma_b_noise);
    log_class[2] = log(pi[2])
                 + normal_lpdf(d[s]      |  mu_d,    sigma_d_sig)
                 + normal_lpdf(beta_s[s] |  mu_beta, sigma_b_sig);
    log_class[3] = log(pi[3])
                 + normal_lpdf(d[s]      | -mu_d,    sigma_d_sig)
                 + normal_lpdf(beta_s[s] | -mu_beta, sigma_b_sig);
    real lse = log_sum_exp(log_class);
    for (k in 1:3) p_class[s, k] = exp(log_class[k] - lse);
  }

  for (t in 1:N) {
    real lp = c[subj[t]]
            + d[subj[t]] * true_target[t]
            + beta_s[subj[t]] * sim[t]
            + bST * site[t]  * true_target[t]
            + bOT * order[t] * true_target[t]
            + bS  * site[t]
            + bO  * order[t];
    real p_eng = Phi(lp);
    real p_obs = (1 - p_lapse) * p_eng + p_lapse * 0.5;
    log_lik[t] = bernoulli_lpmf(said_target[t] | p_obs);
  }
}
"

# Compile and fit
m5_mod <- cmdstan_model(write_stan_file(m5_stan_code))

m5_fit <- m5_mod$sample(
  data            = m5_data,
  chains          = chains_to_use,
  parallel_chains = cores_to_use,
  iter_warmup     = 1500,
  iter_sampling   = 5000,
  adapt_delta     = 0.95,
  max_treedepth   = 12,
  seed            = 2026
)})
```

```{r oberlin-fullsentbayesian }

# Proportion of posterior samples where the effect is positive (interpretable as the probability that oberlin_full > 0) 
post <- extract.samples(m1_acc)
oberlin_full <- post$a_bar + post$bSite + post$bB_bar + post$bB_site
```

**Report 89% compatibility/credible intervals for all your parameter estimates.**

```{r credible-intervals }
# Pull 89% credible intervals for the population-level parameters from each model and stack them into one table. 
# so we can eyeball M2 vs M3 vs M4 vs M5
# Goal is to see size of d_bar / bBT / bBST differences relative to the credible intervals

# Helper function
# extract posterior samples for a list of params from one fit and get data frame with median and CIs
ci_table <- function(fit, params, model_name) {
  
  # pulls the full posterior as a named list 
  post <- extract.samples(fit)
  
  # lapply over the param names so we can handle missing ones
  out <- lapply(params, function(p) {
    x <- post[[p]]
    
    # skip params that arent in this model (e.g. p_lapse in M2)
    if (is.null(x)) return(NULL)
    
    # 89% CI = central interval bounded by the 5.5th and 94.5th percentiles
    q <- quantile(x, probs = c(0.055, 0.5, 0.945))
    
    # one row of the output table per param
    data.frame(model = model_name, param = p,
               median = round(q[2], 3),
               lo89   = round(q[1], 3),
               hi89   = round(q[3], 3),
               row.names = NULL)
  })
  
  # bind rows into a single df
  do.call(rbind, out)
}

# same wrangling but for cmdstanr fits 
# M5 uses cmdstanr because SUPRISE SUPRISE rethinking haaaattttessss discrete mixture + marginalization
ci_table_cmdstan <- function(fit, params, model_name) {
  out <- lapply(params, function(p) {
    s <- tryCatch(fit$summary(p, ~quantile(.x, c(0.055, 0.5, 0.945))),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(s) || nrow(s) == 0) return(NULL)
    data.frame(model = model_name, param = p,
               median = round(s$`50%`, 3),
               lo89   = round(s$`5.5%`, 3),
               hi89   = round(s$`94.5%`, 3),
               row.names = NULL)
  })
  do.call(rbind, out)
}


# parameter lists
# M1 is log odds and doesnt have an SDT parameterization
m1_params <- c("a_bar", "bB_bar", "bSite", "bOrder", "bB_site", "bB_order",
               "sigma_a", "sigma_bB")

# M2 and M3 share the full set of block / site / order interaction terms (full dataset).
# M2 has no p_lapse but ci_table skips missing params
m2_m3_params <- c("c_bar", "d_bar",
                  "bBT", "bST", "bOT", "bBST", "bBOT",
                  "bB", "bS", "bO", "bBS", "bBO",
                  "sigma_c", "sigma_d", "p_lapse")

# M4 is full_sentence only with beta_truetarget.
# beta_bar / sigma_beta added.
m4_params <- c("c_bar", "d_bar", "beta_bar",
               "bST", "bOT", "bS", "bO",
               "sigma_c", "sigma_d", "sigma_beta", "p_lapse")

# M5 is the mixture and reports the mixing proportions and the class-level means/SDs instead of d_bar/beta_bar.
m5_params <- c("c_bar", "p_lapse",
               "pi[1]", "pi[2]", "pi[3]",
               "mu_d", "mu_beta",
               "sigma_d_sig", "sigma_b_sig",
               "sigma_d_noise", "sigma_b_noise",
               "bST", "bOT", "bS", "bO")

# Stack all models' CIs into a table
# (model x param) rows so we can grep/filter/whatever we want after
ci_all <- rbind(
  ci_table(m1_acc,                   m1_params,    "m1_acc"),
  ci_table(m2_sdt,                   m2_m3_params, "m2_sdt"),
  ci_table(m3_sdt_mix,               m2_m3_params, "m3_sdt_mix"),
  ci_table(m4_full_beta,             m4_params,    "m4_full_beta"),
  ci_table_cmdstan(m5_fit,           m5_params,    "m5_mix")
)
ci_all
```

## 3B. Describe/interpret your results

**What do you learn from comparing your models' coefficients?**

____________________________
The main thing I learn from comparing M1 to M2/M3 is that the original accuracy result survives in direction, but that the Bayesian model decomposes the results into the constiituent pieces. Te Oberlin-full composite has 86% posterior mass above zero with an 89% interval that just barely includes zero. So it does seem to be pointing the same way as the original NHT result, but the bayesian model is not quite as confident. Since accuracy is a mixture of sensitivity and criterion, and separating those two is exactly the point of doing SDT instead of just modeling correct/incorrect responses. In this task, target and distractor trials are balanced, so a criterion shift alone cannot generate above-chance accuracy because shifts in  criterion will just trade hits for false alarms. The sensitivity terms in M2/M3 should therefore be what is carrying the NHT accuracy interpretation. In M2, $b_{BT} = 0.07$ $[-0.07, 0.24]$ and $b_{ST} = 0.11$ $[-0.01, 0.23]$ are small and positive, while $b_{BST} = 0.00$ $[-0.16, 0.17]$ so we see that each term is below chance and that the Oberlin full_sentence $d'$ effect is not being driven by some unique Block, Site and TrueTarget interaction, but instead by the accumulation of small additive sensitivity shifts (Block and Site) that, when summed, produce a modestly positive $d'$ in that cell.M3 tells the same story: $b_{BT} = 0.06$ $[-0.13, 0.25]$, $b_{ST} = 0.12$ $[-0.03, 0.26]$, and $b_{BST} = 0.03$ $[-0.18, 0.22]$. So the accuracy result is not only “criterion” and its not attributable to any piece of that interaction in particular. It appears to be coming from some addition of these factors, and there is an interesting finding in seeing the criterion/bias shift. ALthough the criterion shift cannot effect accuracy (and it seems d prime still remains), we seem to see some sort of correlation between the Oberlin sensitivity patterns and genuine signal sensitivity. This matters theoretically because hallucination and perceptual-bias work often finds response bias effects without sensitivity effects, including Bentall and Slade’s auditory SDT study, but here it seems we get both. The  accuracy and dprime is not explained away by criterion/response bias, so there seems to be some sensitivity effect because of the balanced base rates (criterion/bias CANNOT affect accuracy).

The separate criterion finding is does seem to hold up across models. In M2, $b_S = -0.17$ $[-0.28, -0.04]$ and $b_{BS} = 0.11$ $[0.01, 0.19]$ so both exclude zero. In M3, we see the same pattern with the parameter estimates of $b_S = -0.21$ $[-0.36, -0.06]$ and $b_{BS} = 0.13$ $[0.02, 0.23]$. This means Oberlin subjects are more conservative about saying “target” than UChicago subjects, and that site difference becomes smaller in the full_sentence block. The key point, though, is that this is a separate finding. It does not explain the accuracy or $d'$ result. Because target and distractor trials are balanced, criterion shifts cannot produce above-chance performance. So the bayesian approach was able to uncover that there are two things happening at once: there is a modest sensitivity signal (coming from the additive $b_{BT}$ and $b_{ST}$ terms), and there is a site-related difference in response bias.

M2 to M3 shows that adding a lapse component does not change this story. M3 estimates $p_\text{lapse} = 0.17$ $[0.04, 0.34]$, so the model allows for a nontrivial proportion of lapse-like responding, which is plausible in a near-threshold task (i have piloted this thing like 4 times and i zoned out alot). However, the sensitivity and criterion coefficients are not very different from M2. This suggests that, even thought lapses are present, the results survive the idea that subjects may be zoning out on occasion. It is also suprising that the lapse coefficient is so high, given that performance is close to chance, so the model should only have a limited ability to distinguish guesses/attentional lapse from perceptual errors/signal insensitivity. The lapse term absorbs a bit of noise but neither reveals signal nor destroys the existing results.

M3 to M4 is where the model we kind of go out on a limb. I would argue that restricting to the full_sentence block is justified because the flip hypothesis only makes sense when there is at least some usable signal. Adding the per-subject alignment slope $\beta_s$ is also theoretically motivated: if subjects are systematically tracking the stimulus signal in the wrong direction (if you heard these stimuli you would immediately understand that it would be easy to flip these labels), $\beta_s$ should be negative. But in practice, the data does not agree with this hypothesis. M4 yields $\beta_\text{bar} = -0.56$ $[-6.10, 4.93]$ which is very wide, and the sensitivity intercept also becomes much more uncertain ($d_\text{bar} = 0.05$ $[-0.38, 0.47]$). So while M4 better matches the theoretical question, it is not really returning any confident statement about what is going on here. It could be that this effect does not exist, and it could also be that this is underpowered in this dataset. Whatever it is, the posterior is not confident.

M4 to M5 takes the same issue but tries to analyze it using a mixture model. M5 estimates $\pi_\text{flipped} = 0.15$ $[0.02, 0.46]$, so the population-level posterior is compatible with a nonzero proportion of flipped subjects. However, the individual-level class probabilities are diffuse, and model comparison shows no meaningful improvement over M4. This means the mixture prior is more confident than M4 but also does not have much to say. My takeaway is that the data are consistent with the existence of flipped subjects (and also consistent with not-flipped subjects), but we really do not provide have enough data for the model to latch onto such that it can identify them or strongly prefer the mixture model over the simpler alternative.
____________________________

**Based on model evaluation metrics, are you confident that your models are not overfitting or underfitting? Why? Consider comparing overfitting measures and also R-sqrd measures.**

____________________________
The model comparison results suggest that I am not overfitting, but also not gaining much by adding complexity. However it is certainly possible that I am underfitting given the complexity of these models and that we do not have large number of subjects. This is ok to me since I wanted to use this assignment as an opportuinity to flesh out some ideas and approaches. At a later point I will come back and try to refine these. Regardless, M2 and M3 are more or less the same, with $\Delta \text{elpd} = -0.1$ and SE $= 0.7$ under both WAIC and PSIS-LOO, and all Pareto-$k$ values are below 0.7. This suggests that the cross-validation estimates are stable and that neither model is overfitting in a way that harms prediction. The effective number of parameters is also modest relative to the number of trials ($p_{\text{waic}} \approx 33$ for $N = 7748$), which further suggests that the models are not overly flexible.

Similarly, M4 and M5 are indistinguishable ($\Delta \text{elpd} = -0.2$, SE $= 0.5$), so the mixture model is not improving predictive performance despite adding structure. This reinforces the idea that M5 is not overfitting in a catastrophic way, but also not extracting additional signal from the data. Overall, the models appear to be doing ok in terms of the bias–variance tradeoff since they converge and are able to capture the structure of the data, but adding additional complexity did not translate into better model performance.

I do not report Bayesian $R^2$ here because it is not particularly meaningful for this probit SDT setup. The primary question is not variance explained, but predictive accuracy on binary trial outcomes, which is better captured by WAIC and PSIS-LOO. The only caveat is the $\sigma_d$ funnel issue in M2/M3, which affects sampling efficiency but not the overall stability of the population-level estimates. For my final run before submitting I am upping the iterations and warmup runs to see if this helps bring down RHAT and achieve slightly more stable chains. M4 resolves this with a non-centered parameterization, so I am comfortable trusting the main inferences.
____________________________

**Interpret your parameter estimates along with their 89% credible intervals. What kind of inferences can you draw (e.g., causal or non-causal)?**

____________________________

The parameter estimates reinforce the decomposition described above. On the sensitivity side, all of the main coefficients ($b_{BT}$, $b_{ST}$, $b_{BST}$) have 89% credible intervals that include zero, so there is no single effect that can be cleanly labeled as “present” in isolation. However we can see that $b_{BT}$ and $b_{ST}$ are consistently positive across M2 and M3 which means that their sum produces a modest positive $d'$ in the Oberlin full_sentence cell. So the joint pattern matters more than any individual coefficient. In terms of inference, the Block × TrueTarget effect ($b_{BT}$) can be given a causal interpretation because Block is randomized within subject, but the Site-related terms ($b_{ST}$, $b_{BST}$) are observational and should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects (unless grant money is on the line).

On the criterion side there is more to say. Both $b_S$ and $b_{BS}$ exclude zero in M2 and M3 which suggests a reliable difference in response bias between sites and a moderation of that difference by Block. These effects involving Site are still non-causal, but they are clearly present in the data. The key takeaway is that sensitivity and criterion are behaving differently: sensitivity effects are weak and additive, while criterion effects are stronger and more clearly identified.

In M4 and M5, the parameters associated with the flip hypothesis are highly uncertain with wide CIs. The wide interval on $\beta_{\text{bar}}$ and the diffuse mixture weights indicate that the data do not constrain these quantities. As a result, we can only make weak population-level statements (e.g., the data are compatible with some flipped subjects... and also the alternative) and cannot draw confident conclusions about individual-level behavior. Overall, the credible intervals show that the main sensitivity finding is subtle and distributed across parameters, while the criterion effect is more robust, and that more complex hypotheses (like flipping) are not able to be tested via this dataset.

# 4. Discussion

**Write a brief discussion (2-3 paragraphs) that summarizes your findings and interprets the meaning of your findings. Please address:**

- Can causal inference be drawn? Why or why not?

- Discuss some limitations of your study.

- Discuss what future directions you would like to take the work.

____________________________
The main takeaway from this project is that the original NHT result survives, albeit in a weakend form. It would probably be more fair to call it a trend. I am still unsure exactly what is driving it or how to interpret that. This Oberlin full_sentence effect certainly still points in the same direction, but instead of a clear interaction, it seems to decompose into small additive sensitivity shifts that coem together to produce above chance results (according to NHTs). However since criterion cannot actually drive accuracy or dprime in a balanced target/distractor paradigm, we see that there is an indepoendent criterion/bias effect. In particular, this criterion pattern seems to show most prominently across sites. Oberlin subejcts are more hesitant about responding "target", which could come from their student body having a disproportionate amount of musical training, thus enabling subjects to have better auditory timing and thus be able to follow the stimulus "envelope". Being able to follow the envelope would make them better able to know which part of the word "wall" they should be listening for at each timepoint while they are listening to the stimulus. This could then result in the ability to above-chance identify which stimuli are meant to be targets and which stimuli are meant to be targets. Under the (large) assumption that the mixture model from M5 is NOT just underpowered/model is underfit (i.e. the results of this model would be the same even with more subjects), we would also conclude that "anyone who can separate the targets from the distractors knows which group is meant to be the targets and which group is meant to be the distractors". This would rule out the idea that subjects with high accuracy or dprime are just forgetting the template "Wall" and dedicating their energy to trying to find any difference between the groups of stimuli, independent of label. This chain of analysis and assumptions would suggest that the ability to do this task well comes from the ability to find these tiny bits of correlation in the targets and notice their absence in the distractors! It is hard to explain if you don't know this background or haven't experienced the extent to which ALL of the stimuli sound like nothing (when you actually hear these stimuli it seems like it would be GENUINELY IMPOSSIBLE to discern between the two groups), but this has been an open question and this data does provide some genuinely helpful clues for next steps.

So the data are not just showing response bias, and they are not just showing sensitivity either. They show both, but in different ways: a modest sensitivity signal that only becomes visible when terms are combined, and a clearer site-related difference in response bias. The flip hypothesis, which I thought was one of the more theoretically interesting questions, ends up being inconclusive, but as mentioned above there is a potenitally interesting story to tell if we had more data. The data are consistent with the existence of flipped subjects, but also consistent with the non existence of them. Both would tell an interesting story, even though I only expanded on the implications of the latter in the above analysis. As it stands, these models with this data cannot resolve this question or make any judgements about mixture vs simpler alternatives.

In terms of causal inference, only the within-subject manipulated variables (Block, BlockOrder, and trial-level TrueTarget) can support causal interpretations. Effects involving these variables, like the Block × TrueTarget sensitivity shift, can reasonably be interpreted as causal because they were randomized. In contrast, Site is observational, so any Site-related effects (including the criterion shift and Site × TrueTarget sensitivity terms) should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects. There is an unobserved confound $U$ here, which could include things like attention, auditory ability, absorption, or hallucination-proneness, and that backdoor path is not blocked in this analysis.

There are several important limitations. First, the sample size is small ($N = 26$, 16 in oberlin full sentence which is where most of our signal was found), which makes it difficult to identify subject-level parameters, especially in a near-chance task. Second, the stimuli are extremely weak, so each trial carries very little information, which limits the model’s ability to distinguish between sensitivity, bias, and lapses. Third, the sample is restricted to undergraduates from two sites, which limits generalizability and makes the Site effect especially vulnerable to confounding. For future work, I would want a larger and more diverse sample, potentially including participants with higher listening experience/auditory expertise, hallucination-proneness, as well as stimuli with slightly stronger signal to improve identifiability. In further analyses and once I have thought through this extremely long data analysis, I would like to refine this approach so that the models are able to target the relevant questions more directly, and incorporate questionnaire analyses (reducing the scope of U). Furthermore, these and further analyses could result in having a better theoretical ground for the  external measures (e.g., questionnaires or neural data) that we choose, and thus help clarify the latent factors driving sensitivity,bias, and relationships between them. A moreso theoretically driven approach such as this (assuming the theory is correct) would make it possible to more directly test various hypotheses (such as the flip effect rather) than relying soley on weak behavioral signatures.
